en: Having approached Manu as he sat with a one-pointed mind, the great seers honored him according to custom and spoke these words.
O Blessed One, you ought to tell us the duties of all the social classes in their proper order, as well as those born from intermediate unions.
For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true purpose and the nature of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Being thus questioned by those great-souled ones, he of immeasurable power duly honored all those great seers and replied, "Let it be heard."
In the beginning, this was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks,
beyond the reach of reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Then the Lord Self-Existent, the unmanifest one who dispels darkness, appeared— his power having manifested this world beginning with the great elements.
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal,
consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself appeared of his own accord.
Desiring to create various kinds of beings, he first emitted water from his own body through meditation; into that water, he cast his seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The waters are called "nara," for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
because they were his first place of motion (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent—
the Puruṣa who was emitted from that is celebrated in the world as Brahman.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One himself,
through his own meditative power, divided that egg into two parts.
From those two fragments, he fashioned the heaven and the earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
And from himself, he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, he produced the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the presiding lord who conceives "I am."
And [he created] the Great Self (mahat), all that consists of the three qualities (triguṇa),
and gradually the five sense organs which are the perceivers of objects.
But having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [substances] of immeasurable power with portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings.
The six subtle elements resort to these constituent parts of form;
therefore, the wise call that form "the body" (śarīra).
Then the great elements, together with their functions, enter that imperishable creator of all beings, along with the mind and its subtle components.
But from these seven immensely powerful beings,
the perishable arises from the imperishable through subtle material particles.
But among these, each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.
But at the beginning, he fashioned the individual names, actions, and distinct conditions of all beings from the words of the Veda itself.
And that Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings,
the subtle host of Sādhyas, and the eternal sacrifice itself.
From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Veda—
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman— for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and the level and uneven terrains.
Desiring to bring these creatures into existence, he emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger.
And for the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.
The minute, perishable particles which are said to constitute the five elements—
along with these, all this universe comes into being in successive order.
Whatever specific duty the Lord first assigned to each being,
that very same task it performed spontaneously, being created again and again.
In the creation, whatever— whether violent or non-violent, mild or cruel, dharma or adharma, truth or falsehood— the Lord ordained for each being, that entered into it of its own accord.
Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, naturally assume their respective characteristics,
so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became male with one half and female with the other; in her, the Lord created Virāj.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person, whom he himself created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this.
Desiring to create living beings, however, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
These seven Manus of immense splendor created the gods,
the classes of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power.
And [he created] the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various classes of Pitṛs.
Lightnings, thunderclouds, and red clouds; rainbows of Indra;
meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and various celestial luminaries of diverse kinds.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, various birds, domestic animals,
wild beasts, humans, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth.
Worms, insects, moths, lice, flies, and bedbugs;
all gadflies and mosquitoes, as well as various kinds of immobile beings.
Thus, by my command, all this— both the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of their ascetic power, each according to his own karma.
But whatever kind of action is proclaimed here for each of these beings,
that I shall describe to you accordingly, as well as the sequence of their birth.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth,
as well as Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans, are born from the womb.
Birds born from eggs, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises, as well as those of similar kinds that are terrestrial or aquatic; Mn 1.44.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, the bug,
and whatever else is similar, are born from moisture and arise from heat.
All stationary beings that sprout from the soil are either those that grow from seeds or those that grow from stems;
these are the plants (oṣadhyaḥ) which perish at the ripening of their fruit and bear many flowers and fruits.
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those which bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*. 1.47.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses,
those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as creepers and climbing plants.
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
These destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, have been declared to end here within this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time.
When that God is awake, the world thus moves;
when he sleeps, his soul at peace, then everything closes its eyes.
While he sleeps in a state of composure, the embodied beings whose nature is action cease from their respective activities,
and the mind falls into exhaustion.
But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.
But having resorted to this darkness, he remains for a long time endowed with the senses;
yet he does not perform his own function, and then he departs from the body.
When, having become as minute as an atom, it enters into a seed— whether stationary or moving— in conjunction with it, then it assumes a physical form.
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that imperishable one perpetually brings to life and causes the destruction of all this world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having composed this treatise, he himself first caused me alone to learn it according to the prescribed rule; I, however, [taught] Marīci and the other sages.
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of it from me without exception.
Then, having been addressed in that manner by the great seer Manu, Bhrigu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those sages: "Listen! (Mn 1.60).
Six other high-souled and most powerful Manus of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu's lineage have each created their own respective progeny.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval, produced and protected this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those make one *kalā*,
thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*, and a day and night consist of as many *muhūrtas*.
The sun divides day and night for both humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the performance of actions.
A month is a day and a night for the ancestors; its division is by the two fortnights.
The dark fortnight is their day for active duties, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep.
For the gods, a year constitutes day and night; their division is as follows:
the northern course of the sun is their day, and the southern course is their night.
Now learn, in brief, the measure of a day and night of Brahmā, and the duration of each of the Yugas in their respective order.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three ages, together with their twilights and twilight-intervals,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
This cycle of four ages (caturyuga) which has been enumerated at the very beginning consists of twelve thousand [years]; this is called an age (yuga) of the gods.
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation,
should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration.
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration.
At the end of that day and night, he who was asleep awakens;
and having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth the creation;
from that, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure, powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.
From wind, too, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness;
it is radiant and is said to have the quality of form.
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise, having taste as its quality;
from water, earth arises, having smell as its quality—such is the creation from the beginning.
That divine age (yuga) which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years],
multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a manvantara.
Countless Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution,
the Supreme Lord performs again and again, as if in play.
In the Kṛta age, the entire Dharma exists in its four quarters, and truth alone prevails;
no acquisition whatsoever occurs for men through unrighteousness.
In other [ages], Dharma exists by means of traditional scripture, but it is diminished quarter by quarter;
through theft, falsehood, and deceit, Dharma likewise departs quarter by quarter.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, have all their goals accomplished, and live for four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
The lifespan of mortals declared in the Vedas, as well as the blessings resulting from ritual acts and the power of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to the respective age.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, others in the Tretā and Dvāpara,
and still others in the Kali age, in accordance with the decline of the ages.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone is supreme.
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
Protecting the subjects, giving gifts, performing sacrifices, studying the Vedas, and non-attachment to sensual objects— this, in brief, is the duty of a Kṣatriya.
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifice,
study, trade, money-lending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya.
But the Lord ordained only one duty for the Śūdra:
to serve these very castes without malice.
A person is declared to be more pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been called the most pure by the Self-Existent One.
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation.

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the gods always consume as sacrificial offerings (havya) and the ancestors as ancestral offerings (kavya)? (Manu 1.95)
Among beings, the living creatures are the best; among living creatures, those who live by their intelligence;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, the Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brahmins, those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined;
among those of refined intellect, those who perform their duties; and among those who perform their duties, those who know Brahman.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born on earth,
he is born as a lord over all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
Everything that exists in this world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble birth, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this.
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brahmin’s compassion that other people enjoy their sustenance.
For the sake of discerning the karma of that [creation], the wise Manu, son of the Self-Existent, composed this treatise for the remaining [topics] in their proper sequence.
This must be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa,
and it must be correctly expounded to his pupils by him alone, and not by anyone else.
A Brāhmaṇa who studies this treatise and whose vows are well-proclaimed is never tainted by defects of action arising from mind, speech, or body.
He purifies his row of kin, seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even alone, he is worthy of this entire earth.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this brings fame and long life; this is the supreme means to the highest good.
In this [work], Dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions,
and the eternal conduct of all four social classes.
Conduct is the supreme dharma, both that which is declared in the Śruti and that which is prescribed in the Smṛti;
therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda;
but one who is endowed with right conduct shall partake of the full reward.
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages adopted right conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.
And [he shall explain] the origin of the world, the rules for the formative factors (saṃskāra),
the practice of religious observances (vratacaryā) and their application, and the supreme rule for ritual bathing (snāna).
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages,
the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of a Snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, purity, and the purification of objects.
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation;
as well as the entire duty of kings and the legal determination of lawsuits.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife,
the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns [criminals].
The conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for penance; Mn 1.116.
The course of transmigration, which arises from the threefold action,
as well as the supreme good resulting from actions and the examination of their merits and defects.
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and assemblies.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so now do you also learn it from me.
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are ever free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart.
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet there is no such thing as being entirely free from desire in this world;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices originate from volition;
and vows, as well as the duties of self-restraint—all these are traditionally held to be born of volition.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
Behaving correctly toward these, one goes to the world of the immortals and enjoys here all desires exactly as they were intended.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it,
the practice of the virtuous, and also self-satisfaction.
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge.
But having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge,
the wise man, relying on the authority of the revealed scripture, should indeed be established in his own duty.
For a human being who practices the dharma declared in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Smṛti is indeed the Dharmaśāstra;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them the Dharma shone forth.
Any twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would show contempt for their source,
should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda.
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—
they say that this fourfold set is the direct definition of Dharma.
For those who are unattached to wealth and pleasure, the knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the Veda is the supreme authority.
But where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of those are rightly declared as Dharma by the wise.
Whether the sun has risen, or not yet risen, or at the time when night and day meet—sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.
He for whom the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral pyre have been prescribed by means of mantras—
only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
which was created by the gods, they call Brahmāvarta.
Whatever custom has been handed down by tradition in that region for the social classes and the intermediate castes is called "right conduct" (sadācāra).
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣideśa), which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
From a high-born man born in this land,
all men on earth should learn their respective duties.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
and between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the source of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body, beginning with the rite of impregnation, must be performed through meritorious Vedic rituals; it leads to sanctification both in this world and after death.
By means of domestic fire-oblations, the birth-ceremony, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle,
the taint derived from seed and the taint derived from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born.
By the study of the Vedas, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the knowledge of the three Vedas, by sacrifices, by sons,
and by the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.
For a male child, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it includes the ceremonial feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
One should have his naming ceremony performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible.

The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end with a word denoting happiness (*śarman*); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word signifying protection (*rakṣā*); that of a Vaiśya should be connected with a word for prosperity (*puṣṭi*); and that of a Śūdra should be connected with a word for service (*preṣya*).
For women, [the speech] should be easy to pronounce, gentle, clear in meaning, charming, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction.
In the fourth month, the child's first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food, or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to the law in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Vedas.
One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception; and for a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception.
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a Kṣatriya seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya desiring worldly prosperity in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not pass beyond the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa,
nor beyond the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, nor beyond the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya.
Beyond this time, all three of these, if they remain uninitiated according to the prescribed period, become Vrātyas who have fallen from the Sāvitrī and are censured by the Āryas.
A Brāhmaṇa must never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules.
Students of sacred knowledge should wear, in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat; likewise, they may wear garments made of hemp, flax, or wool.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.
In the absence of muñja grass, however, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass,
with three strands knotted together by one, three, or five knots.
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads.
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staves of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, those of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, those of Pīlu or Udumbara.
The staff of a Brahmin should be made to reach the hairline in length;
that of a king (Kṣatriya) should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose.
All those [reeds] should be straight, without blemishes, pleasant to behold,
not causing alarm to men, with their bark intact, and undamaged by fire.
Having taken up his desired staff and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and then go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go about for alms using the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, at the end.
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt, or from her who would not treat him with contempt.
Having collected that alms-food with sincerity, as much as is needed,
and having offered it to his teacher, he should eat while facing the east, pure and having sipped water.
Eating while facing the east promotes longevity; facing the south brings fame;
facing the west brings prosperity; and indeed, facing the north, one eats according to the cosmic order (ṛta).
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
after eating, he should likewise sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these.
One should not give the leavings of food to anyone, nor should one eat between the prescribed meal times;
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from a meal.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to heaven;
it is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
or he may use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya tīrtha.
They declare that the base of the thumb is the Brāhma-tīrtha;
the tip of the fingers is the Kāya; the tip of the hand is the Daiva; and the area below those two is the Pitrya.
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should also touch the cavities of the head with water, as well as the body and the head itself.
One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand, in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north.
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity.
When the right arm is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*.
Having cast his girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya it is in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya it is considered to be two years later than that.
But this entire series of rites for women must be performed without mantras, for the sake of purifying the body at the proper time and in the proper order.
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
their service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and the tending of the sacred fires is their domestic duty.
This has been declared as the sacred rite of initiation for the twice-born, which manifests their true birth; now learn the application of their duties.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.
But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north,
he should be made to study with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light clothing, and with his senses subdued.
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the hands together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
But when the pupil is about to begin his recitation, the teacher, always free from sloth, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when the pupil says, "May there be a pause."
A Brahmin should always utter the syllable Om at the beginning and at the end of his recitation;
for that which is not preceded by Om flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by purificatory rites,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (Manu 2.76)
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times, a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One who is devoid of this Ṛc, and fails in his own duties at the proper time,
being born of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes, incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without sloth reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and having the ether as his form.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as difficult to attain, for it is both Brahman and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (vidhiyajña);
that which is whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña),
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brāhmaṇa attains perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven organs which the wise of old have spoken of.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
Of these, the five sense organs are the ear and so forth in their respective order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth.
The eleventh, the mind, should be known as having a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
Whether one should attain all these [desires] or abandon them entirely,
the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
These senses, when addicted to their objects, cannot be so effectively restrained by abstinence as they can by constant application to knowledge.
Neither the Vedas, nor renunciation, nor sacrifices, nor observances,
nor austerities ever lead to success for one whose inner disposition is corrupted.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor is dejected, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
But if among all the senses even one sense leaks,
through that his wisdom flows away, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind,
he should accomplish all his goals through yoga without wasting his body.
One should stand during the morning twilight reciting the Sāvitrī until the sun appears;
but one should sit during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible.
Standing and reciting during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night;
but sitting during the evening twilight, one destroys the impurity created by the day.
But he who neither remains at the morning [prayer] nor performs the evening [prayer] should be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
Restrained and established in the daily rule near water,
he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Sāvitrī.

Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding days unfit for study (anadhyāya) in the case of the Vedāṅgas, in the daily private recitation (svādhyāya), and indeed in the mantras used for burnt offerings (homa). (Manu Smṛti 2.105)
In the daily obligatory recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as a "Brahma-sacrifice";
it is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* of the suspension-less recitation.
For him who, self-restrained and pure, studies his own sacred texts for a year according to the prescribed rule,
this [fire] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, the twice-born man should, until his formal return home (samāvartana), tend the sacred fire, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher.

The son of a teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman— these ten are to be taught according to the law.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should conduct himself among people like one who is dull-witted.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two dies or incurs enmity.
Where neither dharma nor wealth are found, nor even the corresponding service,
there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in saline soil.
A teacher of the Veda should rather die along with his knowledge;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to a scorner, so that I may remain most powerful. (Manu 2.114)
But speak to that brahmin alone whom you know to be pure, disciplined in his student life, a guardian of the treasure, and vigilant.
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission becomes guilty of stealing the Veda and falls into hell.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge,
one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all things, and sells all things.
One should not sit upon a bed or seat already occupied by a superior;
while staying on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and salute him.
For the vital breaths of a youth indeed depart when an elder approaches;
one recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase: life span, merit, fame, and strength.
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name. (Mn 2.122)
To those who do not know how to address him by name,
a wise man should say "I am he," and the same applies to all women.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is the essential form of names.
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one";
and at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with a protracted (pluta) first syllable.
A Brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be greeted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, regarding his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, regarding his prosperity; and a Śūdra, regarding his health alone.
One who knows the law should address an initiated person by name only if he is younger; otherwise, he should address him using the honorifics "bho" or "bhavat" placed before his name.
But toward a woman who is the wife of another and not related by birth,
he should address her as "lady," "fortunate one," or "sister."
Upon rising to greet maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than himself, he should say, "I am so-and-so."
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
The wife of one's brother of the same caste may be saluted every day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the wives of kinsmen and relatives should be saluted.
One should behave toward one's father's sister, one's mother's sister, and one's elder sister as toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they.
Friendship with fellow citizens is based on a ten-year age difference; that with artists, on a five-year difference;
that with Vedic scholars, on a three-year difference; and among those of the same lineage, it is formed even by a very small difference in age.
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; of these two, the Brahmin is indeed the father.
Wealth, kinship, age, sacred action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding.
Among the three [higher] castes, he who possesses the greatest number of qualities and virtues is worthy of honor here, even if he is a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage of life.

Way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one who stands in his tenth decade of life, to one who is ill, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
Among those who have met together, the bath-graduate (snātaka) and the king are to be honored; and between the royal graduate and the king, the graduate receives the honor due to a monarch.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya.
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the child] with food, is called a guru.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as mother and father; one should never bear him malice.
Ten preceptors equal one teacher; a father exceeds a hundred teachers;
but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for the Brahmin, both in this world and after death.
One should know that the birth which occurs when his mother and father produce him together through desire is merely his physical conception within the womb.
But that birth which the teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is true, and it is free from old age and death.
One should know that person as a teacher here in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever assists one with their study, whether it be little or much.
One who effects a Vedic birth and instructs in one's own duty becomes,
according to the law, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child.
The wise child, the descendant of Aṅgiras, taught his elders;
having encompassed them with knowledge, he said to them, "O little sons."
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods about that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them: "The child has spoken what is right for you."
Indeed, the ignorant one is a child, while the giver of sacred knowledge is a father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child" and the giver of sacred knowledge a "father. (Manu Smṛti 2.153)
The seers did not establish dharma by means of years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great.
The seniority of Brahmins is based on knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas on valor,
that of Vaiśyas on grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone on birth.
One does not become an elder merely because one's head is gray;
even if he is young, the gods know him as an elder who has studied the Vedas.
Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three bear only the name.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with a bull,
and just as a gift given to one who lacks knowledge is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
The instruction of living beings toward their own welfare must be carried out through non-violence alone;
and one who desires righteousness should employ speech that is both sweet and gentle.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit that is taught in the Vedānta.
Even when afflicted, one should not be a wounder of others' vital parts, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others;
one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if at poison,
and he should always long for disrespect as if for nectar.
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in comfort and wakes in comfort;
he moves about this world in comfort, while the scorner perishes.
By this sequential method, the twice-born man, having refined his self, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the realization of Brahman while dwelling with his teacher.
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (the Upanishads), must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule.
A twice-born man who desires to perform austerity should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is declared to be the highest austerity for a Brahmin in this world.
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingernails,
who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.
The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still living, along with his descendants.
The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass;
and the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
In that regard, his birth as a Brahmin, which is marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass,
is said to have the Sāvitrī as its mother and the teacher as its father.
They declare the teacher to be a father because of his imparting the Veda;
for no ritual obligation whatsoever is binding upon him until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
He should not utter the Veda except when performing the offering of *svadhā*;
for he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born [into the knowledge] of the Veda.
For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony, the instruction in the observances and the acquisition of the Veda are prescribed to be performed in due order according to the rules.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, girdle, staff, and garment have been prescribed for him, those same items he must use even during his religious observances.
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules,
fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella, as well as lust, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments; Mn 2.178.
Gambling, public scandal, slander, as well as falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and causing injury to another; Mn 2.179.
One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one destroys one's own vow.
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow dung, earth, and kusha grass, as much as required; and he should go out for alms every day.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praiseworthy in their own duties.
One should not beg for alms from the family of one's teacher, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives;
however, if houses belonging to others are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding category in preference for the next.
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, but he must avoid those who have been accused of crimes.
Having fetched fuel-sticks from a distance, he should place them in the open air;
then, unwearied, he should offer oblations with them into the fire every evening and morning.
If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the subsistence of a vow-holder by means of alms is equal to fasting.
In a rite dedicated to the gods, one should eat like those observing a vow; likewise in a rite for the ancestors, one may eat at will when invited, like a seer (ṛṣi); his vow is not thereby violated.
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in this manner.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should exert effort in his studies and in performing what is beneficial for his preceptor.
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always have his right hand raised, maintain virtuous conduct, and remain well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him.
One should not engage in conversation with a reply while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor while facing away.
Standing, one should attend to him who is seated; approaching, to him who is standing; going forth to meet him, to him who is coming toward one; and running after him, to him who is running.
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is at a distance,
bowing down before one who is reclining, and standing by the side of one who is giving instructions.
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat must always be low;
within the teacher's range of vision, he should not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone even in his absence,
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or even slander of the guru takes place,
there one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
From reviling others one becomes a donkey; indeed, a slanderer becomes a dog; one who consumes another's property becomes a worm, and a miser becomes an insect.
One should not honor him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher to the wind or downwind;
nor should one say anything at all that is beyond the hearing of the teacher.
He may sit together with his teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on a palace, on a stone slab, on mats, or on a rock, a wooden plank, or a boat.
When the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
and without being permitted by one's teacher, one should not salute one's own teachers.

In the same way, one's conduct toward teachers of knowledge, toward one's own kinsmen, and toward those who forbid unrighteousness as well as those who impart what is beneficial, must always be constant.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one would toward the teacher himself—
toward the teacher’s sons, toward noble men, and toward the teacher’s own kinsmen.
Whether he be of the same age as the teacher, or even a student, the son of the teacher deserves the same respect as the teacher himself when he is teaching during a sacrificial rite.
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one wash his feet.
The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste should be honored like the gurus themselves;
however, those of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these should not be performed for the wife of one's teacher.
But a young wife of the guru should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.
This is the inherent nature of women: to corrupt men in this world.
Therefore, for the sake of their own welfare, the wise do not place their trust in young women.
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
However, on this earth, a young man may, at his own will, perform the formal salutation to youthful wives of his teachers according to the rule, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives every day and offer salutations,
keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous.
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade,
so does one who is intent on listening obtain knowledge that resides in the teacher.
Whether he be shaven-headed or wear matted hair, or have a single lock of matted hair on his crown,
the sun shall never set or rise while he remains within a village.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.
For he who, while lying down, is overtaken by the setting sun or finds the sun rising over him,
and fails to perform the penance, shall be joined with great sin.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule.
If a woman or a person of lower caste should perform any act that leads to spiritual welfare, one should practice all of that with diligence; and whatever brings him joy, he should also practice.

Some say that righteousness (dharma) and wealth (artha) constitute the highest good; others say it is pleasure (kāma) and wealth, or righteousness alone; or again, wealth alone is the highest good in this world—such is the established position regarding the three aims of life (trivarga).
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with contempt, even by one who is distressed; this is especially true for a Brahmin.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
The suffering that parents endure for the birth of human beings cannot be repaid, even in a hundred years.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times;
for when these three are satisfied, all austerity is accomplished.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
For they are indeed the three worlds; they are the three stages of life (āśramas);
they are the three Vedas; and they are said to be the three sacred fires.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire;
this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, a householder may conquer the three worlds;
radiant with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world;
and by service to one's teacher, one likewise attains the world of Brahmā.
All duties are honored by him who honors these three;
but for him who does not honor them, all ritual actions are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not attend to anyone else;
he should constantly perform service for them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Whatever one may do for the sake of the next world, one should inform them of each such act through thought, word, and deed, without causing them any inconvenience.
For a man's duty is fully accomplished through these three;
this is the supreme dharma directly perceived, while any other is called a secondary dharma.
One who has faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a person of lower status;
likewise, one should accept the highest dharma even from another, and a jewel of a woman even from a lowly family.
Nectar should be taken even from poison; a well-spoken word even from a child;
good conduct even from an enemy; and gold even from an impure place.
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, eloquent speech,
and various arts— these are to be acquired from everywhere.
In times of distress, studying under one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
however, he must follow and serve that teacher for as long as the study continues.
A pupil seeking the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who has not mastered the Veda.
But if he should prefer a lifelong residence in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation of the body.
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the end of his body goes straightway to the eternal abode of Brahmā.
One who knows the Dharma should not offer anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when he is about to perform the final bath and has been authorized by the teacher, he should provide for the teacher's needs according to his ability.
A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, a seat, grain,
vegetables, and garments— one should bring these to the teacher to produce his satisfaction.

But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher's son who is endowed with good qualities, or toward the teacher's wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as toward the teacher himself.
When these are not available, one who is capable of standing, sitting,
and moving about should perfect his own body by performing service to the sacred fire.
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this manner, remaining unbroken in his vow of celibacy,
goes to the highest station and is not born again in this world.
The vow pertaining to the three Vedas requires a student's conduct toward the teacher for thirty-six years;
or it may be half of that, or a quarter, or even until the [Vedas] have been mastered.
Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in the proper order,
and having remained inviolate in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own duty, who inherits the father's Brahmanic estate, and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland.
Having bathed with the permission of his teacher and returned home according to the rule,
the twice-born man shall marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
She who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union.
Even if they are great and prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain,
one should avoid these ten families in forming a marriage alliance.

Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, those with hairy bodies or hemorrhoids, and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy; Mn 3.7.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.

One should not marry a woman named after a bear, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name.

One should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has a pleasing name, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
But a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter).
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] are permitted in descending order.

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra; she and a woman of his own caste (Viś) are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and a woman of his own caste for a Kṣatriya; and those three and a woman of his own caste for a Brāhmaṇa.
For it is taught that, even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is not to be designated as a wife for either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her.
By taking a Śūdra woman to his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are centered primarily upon that [wealth], neither the ancestors nor the gods will eat; nor does he go to heaven.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a Vṛṣalī, who has been defiled by her breath,
and who has procreated upon her, no expiation is prescribed.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four castes, which are beneficial or harmful both in this world and after death.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
I shall declare to you all that which is the lawful duty for each caste, as well as the virtues and vices belonging to each, and the merits and demerits pertaining to procreation.
One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [marriages] in order, and for a Kshatriya four, starting from the lowest;
but for a Vaishya and a Shudra, one should know those same [four] as lawful, excluding the Rakshasa form.
Sages know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of these five, three are declared here to be lawful and two unlawful;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.
Whether performed separately or mixed together, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Having clothed and honored her himself, and having invited a man of learning and virtuous conduct, the giving away of a daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) rite.
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law,
the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite.
Having addressed the words, "May you both perform dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is sexual in nature and arises from passion.
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she cries out and weeps, after having slain, wounded, or broken through [the defenses], is called the Rākṣasa rite.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is the most sinful of marriages, the eighth and lowest, known as the Paiśāca.
For the foremost of the twice-born, the gift of a daughter in marriage with water alone is distinguished;
but for the other castes, it is by mutual desire.
O Brahmins, listen as I proclaim all the specific merits of these forms of marriage that have been declared by Manu for each of them.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has performed meritorious deeds delivers ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin.
A son born of a wife wedded according to the Daiva rite delivers seven generations before and seven after him;
a son born of a wife wedded according to the Ārṣa rite delivers three before and three after; and a son born of a wife wedded according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite delivers six before and six after.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma form, taken in their proper order, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born.
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
But from the remaining improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and the Dharma are born.
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become blameworthy among men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are blameworthy.
The sacrament of taking the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known for the rite of marriage with women of a different caste.
In marriage with a man of higher caste, the Kṣatriya bride should take hold of an arrow, the Vaiśya maiden a goad,
and the Śūdra woman the hem of the garment.

He should approach his wife during her fertile period and always remain devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for sexual pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days.
The natural menstrual period of women is traditionally held to consist of sixteen nights,
together with the four other days condemned by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights are commended.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on the even nights.
A male is born when the semen is in excess; a female when the female element is in excess.
When the two are equal, a neuter is born, or a male and a female twin; if they are deficient or scanty, the opposite occurs.
Avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and the other [four],
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits.
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off the property of women—
whether it be their vehicles or their clothing— are sinners who go to the lowest state.
Some say that in the rite of the Ṛṣis a pair of cattle is the bride-price;
but that is indeed false, for whether it be small or great, it remains nothing other than a sale.
When the kinsmen do not take a fee for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure benevolence.
These women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity for themselves.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual acts there become fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Those houses which female relatives, when not duly honored, pronounce a curse upon,
perish on all sides as if struck by a magical incantation (kṛtyā).
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always honor these women with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at regular ceremonies and during festivals.
In that family where the husband is always content with his wife and the wife likewise with her husband, prosperity is indeed certain.
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight her husband;
and from the lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed.
When a woman is radiant, the entire family shines; but when she does not shine, the whole family indeed does not shine.
Through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas,
and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble families fall into the state of being non-noble.
By means of crafts, trade, and the exclusive offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king.
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras perish quickly through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and through atheism regarding the efficacy of ritual acts.
But families that are enriched by the power of mantras, even if they possess little wealth,
attain the rank of noble lineages and acquire great renown.
In the nuptial fire, the householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rule,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking.
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound [by sin].
For the sake of expiating all of these in due order, the great seers have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to beings; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability is never tainted by the faults of the slaughterhouse, even while living constantly in the home.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the likewise well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these they declare to be the five sacrifices.
Recitation is the *ahuta* offering; the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits (*bhūta*) is the *prahuta*;
the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya-huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*. (Manu 3.74)
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and to rites for the gods;
for it is by being engaged in rites for the gods that one sustains this world of the moving and the unmoving.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Just as all living beings exist by depending upon the wind,
so do all the other stages of life exist by depending upon the householder.
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone through both knowledge and food,
therefore the householder’s stage is the most excellent.
This must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven and absolute happiness in this world— though it is difficult for those of weak faculties to maintain.
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act for them.
One should honor the ṛṣis with the private recitation of the Veda, the gods with oblations according to the rule,
the ancestors with śrāddha rites, men with food, and the elemental spirits with the bali offering.
Day after day, he should perform the *śrāddha* for the ancestors with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing them satisfaction.
For the sake of the ancestral rites among the five sacrifices, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should not feed any Brahmin at all.
A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform an oblation into the domestic fire from the prepared Vaiśvadeva food for these deities, according to the prescribed rule.
First to Agni and to Soma, then to both of them together,
then to the Viśvedevas and to Dhanvantari.
To Kuhū and to Anumati, and to Prajāpati,
and to Heaven and Earth together, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having thus offered the oblation correctly, he should present the sacrificial portion (bali) in all directions, moving clockwise,
to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, along with their followers.
One should throw [food] at the door with the words, "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water with the words, "To the Waters";
one should offer [food] upon the pestle and mortar with the words, "To the Vanaspatis."
One should offer an oblation for Śrī at the head of the bed and for Bhadrakālī at the foot;
one should, however, present the offering for Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
And he should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
One should offer a Bali oblation on the back of the house for the sake of all beings;
furthermore, one should carry all the remnants of the Bali offering to the south for the ancestors.
One should slowly scatter on the ground food for those who have been slaughtered, for outcasts, for dog-cookers, for those afflicted with foul diseases, for birds, and for insects.
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by the straight path to the supreme abode, his very form composed of light.
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
he should also give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge.
Whatever merit a householder twice-born man obtains by giving a cow to his guru according to the prescribed rule,
that same fruit of merit he obtains by giving alms.
One should respectfully offer even alms or a vessel of water, according to the prescribed rule,
to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when given out of delusion by donors to Brahmins who have become like ashes. (Manu Smṛti 3.97)
An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, who are enriched by knowledge and austerity,
delivers one from distress and even from great sin.
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water,
as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Even if one constantly subsists by gleaning grains or offers oblations into the five fires,
a Brāhmaṇa who dwells unhonored takes away all that merit.
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the house of the virtuous.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally called a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore termed a guest.

One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who has come from another village, as well as one who has arrived by chance, when he has presented himself at the house where a wife resides or even where the sacred fires are maintained.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go, after death, to the state of cattle because they were merely givers of food.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without having eaten.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.

One should provide a superior seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance for those who are superior; for those who are inferior, one should provide an inferior amount; and for those who are equal, an equal amount.
But when the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been completed, if another guest should arrive, one should give him food according to one's ability; however, one should not perform the Bali offering [again].
A Brahmin should not announce his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by proclaiming them for the sake of a meal, he is called a "vomit-eater" by the wise.
But for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya is not called a guest in his house; nor are a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, nor even a friend, a kinsman, or a teacher. *Manu Smṛti* 3.110.
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may,
if desired, feed him as well after the Brahmins have finished eating.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at the household as one entitled to the status of a guest,
he should feed them along with his servants, practicing benevolence.
Furthermore, he should, together with his wife, feed with affection other guests such as friends who have come to his house, providing food according to his means and their station.
One should feed these— married women, young maidens, the sick, and pregnant women— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (Manu 3.115)
Then, when the Brahmins and their own servants have finished eating,
the husband and wife may afterwards eat what remains.
Having worshipped the gods, the seers, human beings, the ancestors, and the domestic deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.

One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, an officiating priest, a snātaka, a teacher, a dear father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, provided it has been a year since they were last honored.
