Both a king and a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) who have arrived for the performance of a sacrifice are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the settled rule that this does not apply when there is no sacrifice.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
But having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
The wise know that the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors is the Anvāhārya;
and that should be performed with effort using commendable meat.
In this regard, I shall explain in their entirety which of the best of the twice-born are to be fed, which are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food.
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large company.
Excessive elaboration destroys these five: hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins; therefore, one should not seek elaboration.
This rite for the deceased, known as the ancestral offering (pitrya), is celebrated at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that [rite], it is always considered a worldly duty for the dead.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit thereby, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
he is the proper recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is considered a guest.
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda eat,
a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, rightfully deserves them all according to dharma.
Offerings to the ancestors and sacrificial oblations should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
As many mouthfuls as one ignorant of the mantras swallows at offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya),
so many glowing iron spikes and iron balls shall the deceased (preta) swallow.
Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established with those who are devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) may be given according to the rule to all four classes alike.
If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas but his son has mastered the Vedas, or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered them; Mn 3.136.
One should know the elder of these two to be the one whose father is a learned scholar of the Vedas;
however, the other deserves honor for the purpose of honoring the sacred mantras.
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
That twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend should be fed at the śrāddha.
For him whose ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and oblations (*havis*) are primarily for the sake of friends,
there is no fruit after death from those *śrāddhas* or oblations.
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships through a funeral feast, falls from the heavenly world— such a man is a "friend at the śrāddha."
The Paiśāca form of marriage is declared by the twice-born to be a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) accompanied by feasting;
yet it remains in this world like a blind cow in a house with only one door.
Just as one who sows seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit,
so too a donor who gives an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit.
By giving a sacrificial fee to a learned man according to the rule, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death.
At a śrāddha, one may certainly honor a friend even if he is not distinguished, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by one who hates the giver becomes fruitless after death.
One should diligently feed at a śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his recitation.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at a person's śrāddha,
the satisfaction of that person's ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations.
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya);
however, this secondary rule (anukalpa), which is always practiced by the virtuous, should also be known.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, a sister's son, a father-in-law, a teacher, a daughter's son, a brother-in-law, a relative, as well as the officiating priest and the person for whom he performs sacrifices.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors has arrived, he should examine him with great care.
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs, as well as those who follow the lifestyle of atheists, to be unworthy of offerings made to the gods or the ancestors.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who officiate as priests for a matted-hair ascetic who has not studied the Vedas, nor for one who is weak, nor for a gambler, nor for groups of such persons.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; Mn 3.153.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who neglects the sacred fires, a hater of Brahmins, the elder brother superseded by the younger, and one who belongs to a guild— all these are unworthy of the funeral cake.

One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour— these are unfit to be invited.
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a paid teacher, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one whose teacher is a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka; Mn 3.156.
Having abandoned, without cause, one's mother, father, or teacher; and having entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections. Mn 3.157 [147M]
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a harlot, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; Mn 3.158.
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (such as poison).

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; Mn 3.160.

One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, an insane person, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be avoided.
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare.
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees; Mn 3.163.
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, a defiler of maidens, a cruel man, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for guilds (gaṇas).
One devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, one who is constantly begging,
one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous— these are likewise unworthy.
A sheep-slaughterer, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and one who carries out the dead for a fee— these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid both these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of sitting in the company at a meal.
But a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.
I shall now declare in its entirety that fruit which arises for a donor after death when a gift is given to one unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or the ancestors.

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those such as the *parivetṛ* and others who are unworthy of the company at a meal— that indeed the *rakṣasas* consume.

He who, while his elder brother remains, enters into the union of marriage and the sacred fire-sacrifice, is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him, the woman through whom the marriage is contracted,
as well as the giver and the officiating priest— the five of them all go to hell.
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—
even if she has been appointed according to the law— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Two kinds of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is one born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is one born when the husband is dead.

But those two beings, born in the field of another, cause the destruction of the offerings of sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral gifts (kavya) given by the donors, both in this world and after death.
As many members of a company as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating,
for that many does the foolish giver fail to obtain the fruit of his gift.
A blind man, by looking at [the food], destroys the merit of ninety [donors]; a one-eyed man, of sixty; a leper, of a hundred;
but one afflicted with a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand donors.
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the material gift.
Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, by accepting a gift from him out of greed,
quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood;
a gift given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
That which is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an offering poured into ashes, even so when given to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
But regarding the other unworthy persons mentioned above, who are unfit to sit in the company at a meal,
the wise declare that their food is equivalent to fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born, the purifiers of the row, by whom a row defiled by those unworthy of the company is purified. (Manu 3.183)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the sacred texts],
and who are born of lineages of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the company.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one whose lineage consists of those who have received the gift of the Veda from a Brahmin, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman.

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a reciter, a student of sacred knowledge, one who bestows a thousand gifts, and one who lives for a hundred years— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
When the Śrāddha rite is about to take place, either on the preceding day or on the following day,
he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who are as described above.
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns, and that [offering] shall be his śrāddha.
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.
But the best of the twice-born, having been invited according to the rule for offerings to the gods or the ancestors,
if he somehow transgresses, that sinner shall go to the state of a pig.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a Śūdra woman,
incurs all whatever evil deed the giver has committed.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, ever practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, the highly fortunate Pitṛs are the ancient deities.
Since the origin of all these [occupations] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now those rules by which they are to be practiced.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others, who were the sons of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha— are recorded as the groups of Pitṛs.
The sons of Virāj, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are those of the Marīcis and of the gods.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are traditionally held to be the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among Brahmins they are named Somapas; among Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujas; among Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among Śūdras, Sukālins.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kavyas, the Barhiṣads,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas and the Saumyas, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins.
Furthermore, regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.
From the sages were born the ancestors; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—was produced in due order.
Even water given with faith in vessels made of silver, or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible merit for them.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection.
One should seek that which has the gods at its beginning and end; it should not have the ancestors at its beginning and end.
For one who seeks that which has the ancestors at its beginning and end perishes quickly, along with his lineage.
One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung and should diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south.
For the ancestors are always satisfied by what is given in open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and in secluded places.
When separate seats covered with sacred grass have been prepared,
he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them.
Having seated those irreproachable Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the deities.
Having brought water for them, as well as sesame seeds together with purifiers,
the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire.
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama according to the rule by means of the offering of oblations, he should afterwards fully satisfy the ancestors.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place the offering directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras.
The ancients describe these best of the twice-born as those who are free from anger, easily propitiated, intent on nourishing the world, and to whom the gods look with favor during ancestral rites.
Having circumambulated the fire keeping it to his left, and having performed the entire rite in reverse order,
he should pour water upon the ground with his left hand.
Having formed three balls from that remnant of the sacrificial food, he, being composed,
should offer them facing south according to the very rite prescribed for water-libations.
Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) then, being self-restrained and according to the prescribed rule,
he should wipe that hand on those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāgin).
Having sipped water and turned away from it, having restrained his breath three times slowly,
he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the balls of rice;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should smell those balls of rice in the order they were offered.
Having taken small portions from each of the balls of food in successive order,
he should first cause those very Brahmins who are seated to eat according to the rule.
While his father is still living, however, he should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone;
or else, as in the case of a Brahmin, he may cause his own father to partake in the śrāddha.
If one's father has passed away but the grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father's name and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
"or, being duly permitted, one may perform it oneself at will. (Manu 3.222)
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the sacred grass (pavitra) into their hands,
he should offer them the first portion of that funeral ball (piṇḍa), saying, "May there be *svadhā* for these."
Holding the vessel containing the increased portion of food with both hands,
he himself should slowly place it near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors.
The food that is brought forth while held in both hands,
the Asuras, being evil-minded, suddenly snatch away.
With self-restraint and concentrated mind, he should first place upon the ground the various side dishes such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
Various kinds of food to be chewed and eaten, roots and fruits,
as well as savory meats and fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure,
being pure and extolling all its qualities.
One should never shed tears, one should not become angry, and one should not speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
Tears cause the departed spirits (pretas) to depart; anger, enemies; falsehood, dogs;
contact with the foot, demons; and shaking [the head], evildoers. (Manu Smṛti 3.230)
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without stinginess;
and he should engage in discourses on the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause [the guests] to hear the private recitation of the Veda, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
the narrative legends, the histories, the Purāṇas, and the supplementary texts.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and other edibles, as well as by praising their virtues.
One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
At a śrāddha, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds;
and in this regard, they praise three other qualities: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while maintaining silence;
nor should the twice-born, when asked by the donor, describe the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
The ancestors eat as long as there is heat in the food, as long as those who have restrained their speech continue to eat,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described.
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
a woman in her menses, and a eunuch— these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these [outcastes] at a house-giving, at a meal,
or at an oblation to the gods or the ancestors, that goes to ruin.
The pig destroys [the merit of the gift] by its smell, the cock by the wind from its wings, the dog by the casting of its gaze, and the low-caste man by his touch. (Manu Smṛti 3.241)
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove him as well.
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has approached for the sake of food, he should,
with the permission of the Brahmins, honor him according to his ability.
Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should cast it upon the ground in front of those who have finished eating, scattering it about.

The food-remnants on the *darbha* grass and whatever scattering of food there may be shall be the allotted portion for those who have died an unnatural death and for women who have left their families.
That which remains on the ground as leavings from one who is neither crooked nor deceitful is declared to be the share of the group of servants at a rite for the ancestors.
Until the rite of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) has been performed for a deceased member of the twice-born caste,
one should perform a śrāddha feast without offerings to the gods and offer only a single funeral cake.
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the law,
the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by means of this very same rite.
That fool who, having eaten at a funeral feast (śrāddha), gives the leavings to a Śūdra,
goes headlong to the Kālasūtra hell.
If one who has partaken of a funeral feast (śrāddha) approaches a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) on that same day,
his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement.
Having asked "Was it well-tasted? he should then cause those who are satisfied to sip water;
once they have sipped water, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be happy."
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhā astu!
For the utterance of "svadhā" is the highest blessing in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present them with the remains of the food;
he should act according to what they say, having been authorized by the twice-born.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "It is well-savored" (svaditam); at a rite in a cow-pen, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (rucitam).
The afternoon, as well as *darbha* grass, the preparation of the site,
sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent twice-born men— these are the perfections in rites for the ancestors (*śrāddha*).
Darbha grass, the strainer, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food,
as well as whatever purifying substance was mentioned previously, should be understood as the requisites for the sacrificial oblation.
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned,
and salt not derived from saline soil— these are called sacrificial oblations by their very nature.

Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, restrained in speech, and pure, and gazing toward the southern direction, he should request these boons from the ancestors: Mn_3.258 [248M] "May the ancestors be satisfied; may they have what they desire; may they be free from debt; may they be well-pleased. Having thus requested these boons, he should circumambulate them from left to right and, remaining seated with his face turned toward the south, he should recite the Svadhā invocation. Mn_3.259 [249M] "Svadhā!"—this is the mantra for the ancestors; it is traditionally taught that there is no mantra superior to this. One should offer it at the rite for the ancestors, whether it be a Vedic mantra or one composed by sages. Mn_3.260 [250M] Then, having sipped water and purified himself, he should offer water-libations to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages, as well as to his own self, by means of water drawn from the vessel. Mn_3.261 [251M] He should then feed the Brahmins who are skilled in the Vedas, being gentle and self-restrained; he should give them food according to his ability, along with curds, honey, and ghee. Mn_3.262 [252M] When they have eaten and have sipped water for purification, he should offer them water mixed with sesame seeds for the purpose of removing the remnants; then, after they have been honored, he should dismiss them with the words, "Go when you please. Mn_3.263 [253M] After they have departed, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, prepare food for guests, and eat the remainder together with his kin, being pure and self-restrained. Mn_3.264 [254M] This is declared to be the rule for the monthly ancestral rite (śrāddha); one should always perform it according to this procedure, increasing its excellence according to one's ability. Mn_3.265 [255M] A Brahmin who, knowing this, performs the ancestral rite every month, causes his ancestors and his own self to ascend to the eternal world of Brahman. Mn_3.266 [256M] They say that the monthly ancestral rite is the highest duty; indeed, the ancestors, being satisfied by it, satisfy all their descendants for twelve generations. Mn_3.267 [257M] One should not perform a Śrāddha on the new-moon day during the fortnight of the waning moon; however, one should certainly perform it on the full-moon day, for that is said to be the most excellent. Mn_3.268 [258M] One should avoid performing a Śrāddha on the fourteenth day, as it is a day of terror; yet, if it falls within the fortnight of the waxing moon, one should perform it even then, for that is a day of great fortune. Mn_3.269 [259M] On the eighth day of the fortnight, on the day of the conjunction, on the days of the solstices, on the equinoxes, on the anniversary of the father’s death, and on the day of the full moon—one should perform a Śrāddha. Mn_3.270 [260M] One should also perform a Śrāddha on the day of the sun’s entry into a zodiac sign, on the day of the Viṣuva, on the Vyatīpāta yoga, during eclipses of the sun and moon, and on the anniversary of the father’s birth. Mn_3.271 [261M] By performing a Śrāddha on these auspicious times, one obtains inexhaustible results; likewise, one should perform a Śrāddha on the twelfth day after the father’s death, as it is a time of great fortune. Mn_3.272 [262M] One should avoid performing a Śrāddha on the first, sixth, and ninth lunar days, as well as on the days of the conjunction and the new moon; but on the other days, one should perform it according to the prescribed rules. Mn_3.273 [263M] One should avoid the first lunar day at the beginning of the fortnight, the sixth and ninth days, and the day of the conjunction; on these, one should not perform a Śrāddha, nor should one perform it on the new-moon day during the fortnight of the waning moon. Mn_3.274 [264M] However, if one desires to perform a Śrāddha on the new-moon day, one should do so during the fortnight of the waxing moon; otherwise, one should perform it on the full-moon day, for that is the most excellent. Mn_3.276 [266M] But if one desires to perform a Śrāddha on the new-moon day, one should do so during the fortnight of the waxing moon; otherwise, one should perform it on the full-moon day, for that is the most excellent. Mn_3.287 [277M] One should avoid the first lunar day at the beginning of the fortnight, the sixth and ninth days, and the day of the conjunction; on these, one should not perform a Śrāddha, nor should one perform it on the new-moon day during the fortnight of the waning moon. Mn_3.288 [278M] But
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."

Having thus performed the offering of the water libations, one should immediately thereafter cause those rice-balls to be eaten by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else cast them into the water.
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes only after [the period of impurity];
others cause them to be eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water.
Then, a devoted wife who is the lawful partner of her husband and intent on the worship of the ancestors,
desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of offspring, virtuous, and likewise righteous.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide a meal primarily for his kinsmen;
having given what is honored to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives.
That remnant of food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established.
I shall now describe in its entirety that sacrificial offering which, when given to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for a long time and even for eternity.
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rule,
the ancestors of men remain satisfied for a month.
For two months one may subsist on the flesh of fish, for three months on the flesh of deer,
for four months on the flesh of sheep, and for five months indeed on the flesh of birds.
For six months with the meat of a goat, and for seven with that of the spotted deer;
for eight with the meat of the black antelope, and for nine indeed with that of the Ruru deer.
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boar and buffalo;
however, by the flesh of rabbit and tortoise, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
But by means of cow's milk, milk-rice,
and the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa, one’s satisfaction lasts for twelve years.
Black śāka, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red goat, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for ascetics are prescribed for the sake of infinite results.
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the asterism Maghā.
"May there be born in our family one who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, before the shadow of an elephant has turned."
Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
In the dark fortnight, starting from the tenth day and excluding the fourteenth, these lunar days are recommended for the Śrāddha rite; other days are not so.
By performing [the śrāddha] on odd lunar days and under odd asterisms, one enjoys all desires;
but by performing it on even days, one obtains abundant progeny for all the ancestors.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too is the afternoon superior to the forenoon for a funeral feast (śrāddha).
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the offering properly made from left to right, unwearied,
and holding darbha grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.
One should not perform a Śrāddha at night, for that is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.
By this rule, one should perform the *śrāddha* here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the *pañcayajña* daily.
The oblation pertaining to the sacrifice for the ancestors is not prescribed to be performed in a common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires without the Darśa sacrifice.
When the best of the twice-born, having bathed, gratifies the ancestors with water,
he thereby obtains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
He should always be an eater of vighasa, and he should always be one whose food is amṛta;
vighasa is what remains after eating, and likewise, amṛta is what remains from a sacrifice.
All these rules regarding the five sacrifices have been declared to you;
now hear the rules for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born.
O twice-born ones, having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher,
he should dwell in his house as a married man during the second quarter of his life.
A Brahmin should live in times of non-distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury. (Manu Smṛti 4.2)
For the sake of accomplishing the mere necessities of life,
he should accumulate wealth by means of his own irreproachable occupations, without causing distress to his body.
One may live by means of *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by *mṛta* and *pramṛta*, or even by *satya* and *anṛta*; but one must never live by the "dog's mode of life" (*śvavṛtti*).
Gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains is to be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Begging for alms is called *mṛta*, while agriculture is traditionally known as *pramṛta*.
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may even live by it;
service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or enough for a single jar;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even provide for tomorrow.
Among these four types of twice-born householders,
each subsequent one should be known as superior according to dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmasattra).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭi sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
He should not follow worldly conduct for the sake of livelihood in any way whatsoever; he should live the pure life of a Brahmin, free from crookedness and guile.
Seeking happiness, one who desires ease should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering.
A twice-born Snātaka living by any one of these modes of livelihood should observe these following vows, which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: [Mn 4.13]
One should constantly perform one's own duty as declared in the Veda without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. (Mn 4.14)
One should not seek wealth through excessive attachment, nor by forbidden actions;
nor should one do so from here and there, even when resources are available, much less in times of distress.
One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should also turn back from excessive attachment to them by means of the mind.
One should abandon all pursuits that conflict with Vedic study;
however, one should teach in whatever manner possible, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's duty.
One should conduct oneself in this world by practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage.
He should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, as well as the Vedic Nigamas, for they are auspicious and beneficial.
For in whatever measure a person masters a scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his knowledge shines forth. (Manu Smṛti 4.20)
One should never neglect, according to one's ability, the sacrifice to the seers, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to the ancestors.
Some people who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly desire.
Some offer the breath into speech and speech into breath at all times,
perceiving the inexhaustible accomplishment of sacrifice in both speech and breath.
Other brahmins always perform these sacrifices with knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.
One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night,
as well as the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice likewise.

At the end of the harvest, a twice-born man should satisfy his debt with a sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, with solemn rites; at the beginning of each solstice, with an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, with Soma sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, desiring to live a long life, must not eat new grain or meat without having first performed the sacrifice of the first-fruits and the animal sacrifice.
For his fires, greedy for fresh grain and meat, if not honored with an offering of new grain and animal sacrifice, desire to consume his very life-breaths.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability, whether with seats, food, and beds, or with water, roots, and fruits. (Manu Smṛti 4.29)

One should not honor with even a word or a limb those who follow heretical sects, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, the deceitful, those who rely on mere reasoning, and those who behave like herons.

One should honor with offerings to the gods and the ancestors those householders who are learned in the Vedas, purified by their knowledge, sacred learning, and vows; one should avoid those who are the opposite.
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves,
and he should provide a share to all living beings without causing hardship to his own dependents.

A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; it is the settled rule that he must not seek it from anyone else.
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger if he is capable [of providing for himself],
nor shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes as long as he has the means.
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and to what is beneficial for the self.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot containing water,
the sacred thread, a Veda manuscript, and two auspicious golden earrings.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not step over a calf's tethering rope, nor run while it is raining, nor should one look at one's own reflection in water; such is the traditional rule.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees.
Even if he is intoxicated, he must not approach a woman during her menstrual period,
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish.
For one who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by menstrual flow,
wisdom, vigor, strength, vision, and lifespan indeed increase.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease.
A twice-born man desiring splendor should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth. (Manu 4.44)
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked;
one should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
Neither on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain;
neither in a ruined temple nor on an anthill, never at any time.
He should not study in pits inhabited by living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing;
nor having reached the bank of a river, nor on the summit of a mountain.
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or cows,
one should never discharge feces or urine.
Having covered himself with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or similar materials, he should pass by,
restraining his speech, being pure, with his limbs wrapped and his head veiled.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night, one should face south; and during the two twilights, one should face the same direction as during the day.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purificatory act] facing any direction he finds comfortable, as well as when there is fear of danger to life.
The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man,
or facing a cow or the wind, perishes.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it beneath [one's feet], nor should one step over it;
one should not treat it with the soles of one's feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings.
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor travel, nor lie down;
one should not scratch the ground, nor remove one's own garland.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water,
nor anything else smeared with impurity, nor blood, nor poisons.
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one awaken a superior person;
one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice unless invited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling, nor should one tell anyone [of it];
likewise, a wise man, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone.
One should not dwell in a village that is unrighteous, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one reside for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people,
nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating;
one should not eat too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat in the morning.
One should not engage in futile exertion, nor drink water from one's cupped hands;
one should not eat food while holding it in one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor utter cries when impassioned.
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal;
nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature.
One should not wear sandals, clothing, a sacred thread, an ornament, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (Manu 4.66)
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease,
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are deformed.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without lashing them excessively with the goad.
The morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless labor, nor any action that results in future suffering.
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails,
as well as the slanderer and the impure person, quickly goes to destruction.
One should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should one wear a garland outside [the house];
riding on the backs of cows is in every way condemned.
One should not enter an enclosed village or house by a way other than the gate,
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
When the sun has set, one should not eat anything mixed with sesame seeds;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor go anywhere while still impure from a meal.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one attains a long life.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds, nor cotton seeds, nor chaff.
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with outcastes, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for a sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.
For he who teaches him the Dharma and he who enjoins him to a vow sink together into the darkness called "unrestrained" along with that very person.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using water.
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking others on the head;
furthermore, after bathing the head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse, a cart, or a tavern banner, nor from those who live by prostitution.
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a flagstaff is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten flagstaffs; and a king is equal to ten brothels.
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is terrible.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in due course, go to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the Kālasūtra hell, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pratimūrtika.
The Iron Spike, the Residue of Grain, the Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-Leaves, and likewise the Iron-Brigade.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire their own welfare after death do not accept gifts from a king.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as the bodily afflictions rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, having purified himself and composed his mind,
he should stand for a long time during the morning twilight reciting prayers, and likewise at its proper time for the evening twilight.
By virtue of their long observance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), the seers (*ṛṣis*) attain long life,
as well as wisdom, renown, fame, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being self-controlled, should study the Vedic hymns for four and a half months.
Under the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the formal dismissal (utsarjana) of the Vedas outside [the village],
or on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, in the forenoon.

Having thus performed the formal dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside according to the scriptures, he should cease [recitation] for a night with its two flanking days— that is, for one full day and night.
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and he should study all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas during the dark fortnights.
One should not recite the Veda indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras;
having recited the Veda, one should not sleep again at the end of the night while exhausted.
A twice-born man who is disciplined should always recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule, provided there is no time of distress. Mn 4.100.
One who is studying should always avoid these days unfit for study,
as should one who is teaching disciples according to the prescribed rule.
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when there is a rising of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when great meteors fall,
there shall be an interruption of study for the remainder of the day.

One should know that when these [omens] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, during the wrong season, even at the sight of clouds.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) lasting until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as if it were day.
For those who desire proficiency in Dharma, there shall always be a suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as whenever a foul odor is present.
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a low-caste person (vṛṣala),
nor when there is weeping, nor in a crowd of people.
While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine, while impure from food, or after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony—one should not even mentally contemplate [forbidden things]. (MN 4.109)

Having accepted an invitation to an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the period of ritual impurity following the death of a king or an eclipse of Rāhu.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of food offered to a single ancestor remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda.
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food from a house where a birth-impurity (sūtaka) has occurred.
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon and fourteenth days, and on the full moon and Aṣṭakā days; Mn 4.113.
The new moon day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the eighth day and the full moon day destroy the Veda; therefore, one should avoid them.
A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking or braying in a row.

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a funeral rite (śrāddha).

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony, upon touching that, there is a suspension of study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth.
One should know that there is no study for the remainder of the day when a village is harassed by thieves, when a panic caused by fire has arisen, and during all extraordinary portents.
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
likewise for the Aṣṭakās and on the nights at the end of the seasons, it lasts for one day and night.
One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant;
nor in a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is acidity.
Nor when one has not taken leave of a guest, or while a strong wind is blowing, or when blood is flowing from the body, or when it is wounded by a weapon. (Manu 4.122)
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of the Sāmaveda is being heard;
nor after having completed the study of the entire Veda, nor after having studied the Āraṇyaka.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Knowing this, the learned, having daily first practiced the essence of the three Vedas in due order, afterwards study the Veda itself.
If any of these—cattle, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat—should pass between [the teacher and the pupil], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night. (Mn 4.126)
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study: an impure place for Vedic recitation and an impure self. Mn 4.127.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born Snātaka should always remain celibate, even during the period favorable for conception.
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in a body of water that is unknown.

One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, of one's teacher, of a king, of a *snātaka*, of an *ācārya*, of a tawny person (*babhru*), or of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
At midday and at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should not intentionally step upon the remnants of anointing unguents, the water used for bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this life. (Mn 4.134)
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak.
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
One should not despise oneself because of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak an untruth that is pleasant—this is the eternal dharma.
One should say "May there be welfare, may there be welfare," or simply say "May there be welfare";
one should not engage in dry enmity or dispute with anyone.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.
One should not insult those who have missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor, while remaining in a healthy state, should he look at the hosts of luminaries during the day while still impure.
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily apertures without a specific reason;
he should avoid touching all the hairs of his private parts as well.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and having conquered his senses;
he should constantly mutter prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.
For those who are devoted to auspicious conduct, who are ever self-restrained,
and who perform recitations and fire-offerings, no misfortune exists.
One should constantly study the Veda at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty.
Through constant study of the Veda, through purity, and indeed through austerity—
And by not harming living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Remembering his former birth, he practices Brahman once again;
and through the constant practice of Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss.
One should constantly perform the Sāvitra oblations and the propitiatory fire-offerings on the Parvan days;
and one should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā and Anvaṣṭakā days.
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, as well as the water used for washing the feet and the disposal of leftover food, at a distance indeed.
One should perform the preparation for anointing, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone. (Manu Smṛti 4.152)
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and eminent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his teachers.
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart.
One should, unwearied, constantly practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma and is properly set forth in one's own duties as declared by the Śruti and Smṛti.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in this world;
he constantly partakes of suffering, being diseased and short-lived. (Mn 4.157)
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
Whatever action depends on others, that he should avoid with effort;
but whatever depends on himself, that he should practice with diligence.
"Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering. (Manu Smṛti 4.160)
Whatever action brings satisfaction to his inner self while he performs it, that he should undertake with effort; but he should avoid the opposite.
One should not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a preceptor, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, disparaging the deities,
as well as hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness.
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down;
except for a son or a pupil, whom one may strike for the purpose of instruction.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [a Brahmin] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in miserable wombs.
A man who, through lack of wisdom, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting,
incurs very great suffering after death.
For as many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth,
for that many years shall the shedder of blood be devoured by others in the next world.
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who is constantly devoted to violence— does not find happiness in this world.
Even if he suffers for his righteousness, he should not turn his mind toward unrighteousness,
seeing that the wicked who act contrary to dharma swiftly meet with their downfall.
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
however, turning back slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.
If [the fruit of an action] does not accrue to oneself, it may accrue to one's sons; if not to the sons, then to one's grandsons; but an unrighteous act never fails to bear fruit for the doer.
By unrighteousness one prospers for a while, then one beholds auspicious things;
thereafter one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes along with their very roots.
He should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and he should instruct his pupils in accordance with dharma, restraining his speech, his arms, and his belly.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future unhappiness or is censured by the world.
He should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes; he should not be dishonest, nor fickle in speech, nor intent on actions that harm others.
By that path by which his fathers have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm.

With officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
One should not engage in a dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants.
By renouncing disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati;
but the guest is the lord of the world of Indra and of the world of the gods, as are the officiating priests.

Female relatives reside in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice in the world of the Viśvedevas; maternal relations in the world of the Waters; and one's mother and maternal uncle on the earth.
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords over space;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body.
One's shadow, one's group of servants, and one's daughter are the utmost objects of compassion;
therefore, one should always endure being insulted by them without any resentment.
Even if he is capable of accepting gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, his Brahmanic luster is quickly extinguished.
Without knowing the righteous rule for the acceptance of material gifts,
a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold, life-span, and food; land, a cow, and also the body;
a horse, sight, skin, clothing, clarified butter, splendor, sesame seeds, and offspring—these [purify one who offers them]. (Manu 4.189)
But a twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study the Vedas, and who delights in accepting gifts,
sinks along with that very recipient, like one in water using a stone as a raft.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear whatever gift he might receive;
for even by a very small amount, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat,
nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Veda.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the law, when given to these three types of persons,
results in misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks,
so do both the giver and the recipient sink to the bottom if they lack knowledge.
One who carries the banner of Dharma while being always greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world;
one who acts like a cat, violent, and a betrayer of all—such a person is to be known as a "cat-vowed" hypocrite (baiḍālavratika).
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is cruel, intent on achieving his own ends,
deceitful, and falsely humble, practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata).
Those Brahmins who practice the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful action.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras.
Such Brahmins are censured both in this world and after death by those who discourse on the Veda; and a vow performed through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, being without marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks of an ascetic, takes upon himself the sin of those who wear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the reservoir's builder.
One who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given incurs a fourth part of the sin.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in mountain clefts and springs.
A wise man should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not the observances (niyamas) exclusively;
for by failing to practice the restraints while devoting himself solely to the observances, he falls.

A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one conducted by a priest who officiates for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
This is offensive to the virtuous, wherein these people offer oblations;
it is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it.
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by a foot.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses,
pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit to be eaten].

Food smelled by a cow, and especially food [announced by] public proclamation, food belonging to a multitude, food belonging to a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned; Mn 4.209 [210M].
The food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer, one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, and one bound in fetters; Mn 4.210.
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as sour gruel, stale food, and the leavings of a Śūdra—these must not be eaten.

The food of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, of one who eats leavings, of one who eats the food of a fierce man, of a woman in childbirth, and that which has been tasted by another before being served, as well as food from a house where ten days have not yet passed since a death— these are forbidden.
Meat not consecrated by a ritual, meat obtained in vain, the food of a woman who has no male relatives,
the food of an enemy, the food of a city-dweller, the food of an outcast, and that which has been sneezed upon.
The food of the slanderer and the liar, as well as that of one who sells the results of sacrifices, the food of an actor and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person; Mn 4.214 [215M].
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a goldsmith, a basket-maker, and likewise of a seller of weapons; Mn 4.215 [216M].
From those who keep dogs, from vintners, from a washerman, from a dyer,
from a cruel man, and from one in whose house a paramour resides.
Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely dominated by women,
food from one recently deceased (within ten days), and that which causes dissatisfaction— [these one should avoid].
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's spiritual luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Regarding those others who have been successively proclaimed as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance.
A learned twice-born man should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha);
however, if he has no other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night.
Having deliberated upon both the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer, the gods ordained their food to be equal.
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
the gift of a liberal man purified by faith is [efficacious], while the other is destroyed by lack of faith."
With faith and without indolence, one should constantly perform sacrifices and works of public utility;
for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired by righteous means, those two become inexhaustible.
One should constantly practice the duty of giving— both that which pertains to sacrifices and that which pertains to public works—
with a spirit of complete contentment, whenever one encounters a worthy recipient, according to one's ability.
Whatever may be asked for should be given without malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who will deliver one from all [sins].
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desirable offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of a horse, the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the realm of the Sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of freedom from fear obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Of all gifts—water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter—the gift of the Veda is preeminent. (Manu Smṛti 4.233)
In whatever manner one bestows whatever gift,
one receives that very same thing, honored in return in that very same manner.
He who accepts what has been honored, or he who gives what has indeed been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell.
One should not take pride in one's asceticism; nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice.
Even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, and having given a gift, one should not boast of it.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride;
life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins; and the merit of a gift perishes through boasting of it.
One should gradually accumulate merit, as termites build an anthill,
for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings.
For neither father nor mother stand by one in the next world for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman stands there—dharma alone stands.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds.
Having abandoned the dead body on the ground like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; Dharma alone follows him.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads that man who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity to the next world.
One who desires to lead his family to eminence should always form connections with the most excellent,
and should avoid those who are inferior.
By approaching only the most excellent and avoiding the inferior, a Brahmin attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra.
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
one who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and generosity.
One may accept from anyone fuel for the fire, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered, honey, and the gift of safety.
Prajāpati considered alms that have been brought forward and offered spontaneously, without being previously solicited, as acceptable even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years of him who treats with contempt that [food], nor does the fire carry his oblation.
One should not reject a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, gems, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself must not be satisfied by that alone.
But when his teachers have passed away, or when living at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always receive [gifts] from virtuous persons.
A partner in trade, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—
these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Whatever his own nature may be, whatever he intends to do,
and how he should serve him, in that manner he should present himself.
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is, speaking falsely among the virtuous, is the greatest evildoer in the world; he is a thief who steals his own soul.
All objects of speech are fixed; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech. That man who steals them commits every form of theft.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live adopting an attitude of neutrality.
Alone, one should constantly reflect in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself;
for by reflecting alone, one attains the supreme good.
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder,
as well as the ritual rules for the vows of a Snātaka, which are auspicious and increase one's inner strength.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from all taint and is glorified in the world of Brahma.
Having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, the seers spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: *Manu Smṛti 5.1*
O Lord, how does death prevail over those Brahmins who, as previously described, follow their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the Shastras? (Manu Smriti 5.2)
That righteous Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen, by what fault Death seeks to slay the Brahmins."
Through the neglect of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct,
laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms,
as well as anything produced from impure matter, are not to be eaten by the twice-born.
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions, and the śelu fruit, cow's milk, and colostrum.
One should not eat kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, or cakes in vain, nor meat that has not been consecrated, nor food intended for the gods, nor sacrificial offerings.
The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals, that of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died; Mn 5.8.
And among all wild animals, except for the buffalo, as well as the milk of females and all fermented acids, these indeed must be avoided. (Manu Smṛti 5.9)
Among sour substances, curd is fit for consumption, as is everything produced from curd,
and those [liquors] which are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those that dwell in villages, single-hoofed animals not specifically permitted, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird. (Manu 5.11)
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the village cock, the sārasa, the rajjuvāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina; Mn 5.12.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat; Mn 5.13.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; Mn 5.14.
He who eats the flesh of any creature is said to be an eater of that very creature; a fish-eater is an eater of all kinds of flesh; therefore, one should avoid fish.
