The pāṭhīna and rohita fish are the first ones prescribed for offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
likewise, the rājīva, siṃhatuṇḍa, and all kinds of scaled fish are permitted.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown,
nor any five-toed creatures, even if they are among those designated as edible.
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—
these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel.
Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock,
an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa;
for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, for food known [to be forbidden], the penance must be specifically distinguished.
Excellent wild animals and birds may be slain by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sake of maintaining their dependents; for Agastya did so in ancient times.
For even in ancient sacrifices and in the rites of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) consisted of the edible flesh of wild animals and birds. (Manu Smṛti 5.23)
Whatever food, whether solid or soft, that is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured,
may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as may whatever remains from an oblation to the gods.

Even if it has been kept for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born even if they have not been sprinkled with clarified butter.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what is fit and unfit to be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
One may eat meat that has been consecrated with water, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged in a rite according to the rules, or when one's life is in danger. (Manu 5.27)
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa):
both the stationary and the moving; everything is the sustenance of the vital breath.
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs;
the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave.
The eater is not defiled by eating those living beings who are fit to be eaten, even day after day;
for both the eaters and the beings fit to be eaten were created by the Creator himself.
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance; any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance. (Manu Smṛti 5.31)
Having purchased it, or having produced it himself, or even having received it from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors.
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when there is no distress;
for having eaten meat contrary to the rule, he is helplessly devoured by those very animals after death as a ghost.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great after death as that of one who eats meat in vain.
But that man who, though duly appointed, does not eat meat,
goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated by mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated by mantras.
In times of distress, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the victim, or likewise with a victim made of flour;
but one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death after death in successive births.
Animals were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world, therefore killing in a sacrifice is not killing.
Herbs, animals, trees, crawling creatures, and birds likewise,
having met their end for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher rebirths once again.
"Manu has declared that animals may be slain only in the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods; not elsewhere."
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animal to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
One should know that violence toward the moving and stationary beings which is prescribed by the Veda and regulated in this world is indeed non-violence; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or dead.
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage or death,
seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one performs, and wherever one fixes one's affection—
that one attains without effort, provided that one does not harm anything whatsoever.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should abstain from the eating of all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the manner of a Piśāca,
does not fail to attain popularity in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.

The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it—all these are slayers. (Manu Smṛti 5.51)
There is no doer of more demeritorious deeds than he who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another, without having first worshipped the ancestors and the gods.
He who should perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots or by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'meat-ness' (māṃsatva) of meat."
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
these are the natural inclinations of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit.
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased, as well as the purification of objects,
for all four castes in their proper order and according to rule.

When one has died after the eruption of teeth, after the cutting of hair, or after the tonsure ceremony, all relatives remain impure; the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka). Impurity on account of death (śāva) is ordained for ten days among those who share the funeral oblation (sapiṇḍas).
Until the collection of the bones has taken place, [the impurity lasts] for three days or for one day only.
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka (a distant kinsman) persists as long as there is knowledge of the common ancestry or the name.
Just as this impurity on account of death is prescribed for the sapindas,
so too should it be in the case of birth for those who desire complete purity.
For all others, there is impurity due to death; however, for parents, there is impurity due to birth.
Impurity due to birth belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by bathing.
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by sipping water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three periods of three nights;
those who offer water [for the deceased] are purified after three days.
But a disciple who performs the funeral rites for his deceased preceptor becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse.
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
once her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who has become soiled by it is purified by bathing.
For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is traditionally held to occur after one night;
but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is required after three nights.
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside the village,
having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the rite of collecting the bones.
For him, no funeral rite with fire should be performed, nor should the water-libation be offered;
having abandoned him in the forest like a log, they should observe impurity for exactly three days.
The ritual offering of water should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it for one who has teethed, or once the naming ceremony has been completed.
If a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin) has died, purification is prescribed after one day;
however, for those who share the same funeral water (ekodaka), purity is held to be attained after three nights following the birth [or death].
But for female relatives who have not been consecrated with marriage rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those who share the same ancestry (sanābhayaḥ) become pure according to the very rule already stated.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves for three days,
they should not consume meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground.
This rule for impurity due to death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure for relatives and kinsmen is to be known as applicable when one is absent.
But he who hears that one residing in a foreign land has died within ten days shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights.
When ten days have passed, one remains impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed,
a man becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.
If a child, a person residing in another country, or one who has become a separate individual (by renouncing family ties) dies,
one is purified immediately by immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes.
If death or birth should occur again within ten days,
the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure until that period of ten days has passed.
They say that when an Ācārya has passed away, the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise, it is the settled rule that it lasts for a day and a night in the case of his son or his wife.
Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has arrived as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights;
likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, for a period of a night with its two surrounding days (pakṣiṇī).
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun or stars] lasts;
but if the king is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), the impurity lasts for a full day, as does that for a teacher who has completed his Vedic studies (*anūcāna*).
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires;
and while performing that rite, even a kinsman does not become impure.
Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth,
a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water and become purified, he should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability.
Having touched a human bone that still has fat adhering to it, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of fat, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libations, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
The water libation shall be withheld from those born of illicit unions, from those who persist in heretical ascetic orders,
and from those who commit suicide.
And for women who have taken refuge in heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or preceptor who has died, one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.
One should carry out a dead Śūdra through the southern city gate;
but for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates, as appropriate.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions; for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman.
Immediate purification is prescribed for a king in his high office;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], intended for the protection of his subjects.
And for those killed in a riot, by lightning, or by the king;
for the sake of cows or Brahmins; and for whomever the king desires [to be so].
The king bears the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Apapati, and Yama.
A king who is empowered by Lokeśa is not subject to ritual impurity;
for purity and impurity among mortals arise from and dissolve back into the worlds.
For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons while following the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed, and likewise the period of impurity; such is the settled rule.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, by touching his mount or weapon;
a Vaiśya, by touching his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, by touching a staff.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you;
now learn the purification for the dead concerning all those who are not sapindas.
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the maternal relatives of his mother.
If he eats their food, however, he is purified in ten days;
but if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.
If one follows out of desire a deceased kinsman or even a stranger,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that offering, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay],
wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the means by which embodied beings achieve purification.
Among all forms of purity, purity of wealth is declared to be supreme;
for he who is pure in wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by earth and water.
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts by giving;
those whose sins are concealed by silent recitation; and the best among the knowers of the Vedas by austerity.
That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This determination regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.
The purification of luminous gems, as well as of all stone-made objects,
has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
A gold vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they are not otherwise defiled.
Gold and silver were produced from the union of water and fire;
therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, or water.
For all liquid substances, purification is declared to be straining;
for solid objects, sprinkling; and for wooden articles, scraping.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* and *graha* cups is by washing.
The purification of the *caru* vessels and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is by means of hot water;
so too for the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the cart (*śakaṭa*), and the pestle and mortar (*musala-ulkhala*).
The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is performed by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed.
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is held to be like that of grain.
Silk and woolen cloth are purified with alkaline salts; blankets of Kutapa wool with Ariṣṭaka fruits; fine linen cloth with Bilva fruits; and linen cloth with white mustard seeds.
A wise person should perform the purification of conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory with cow urine or water, just as one would for linen cloth.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by re-baking it.
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus,
or blood can never be purified by re-firing.
The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by smearing with cow-dung, by sprinkling, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows.
Food that has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed upon,
or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
In all purifications of objects, earth and water must be applied as long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart.
The gods have ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word.
Water found on the ground is pure if it is sufficient to quench the thirst of a cow, provided it has not been contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural odor, color, and taste. (Manu 5.128)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the settled rule.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure,
as is the flesh of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and other bandits.
The apertures above the navel are all pure;
those below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body.
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure upon contact.
For the purpose of purifying the voiding of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken as required;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of men.
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand,
and seven on both hands by one desiring purification.
This is the rule of purification for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise, one who is about to study the Veda and always when eating food.
One who desires bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so only once each.
Śūdras who live according to the law must have their hair shaved every month;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of twice-born men.
The mouthfuls of food do not make one impure, nor do the drops that fall upon the body; nor do the hairs of the beard that enter the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth. (Manu 5.141)
Those drops which touch the feet of one who is giving water for sipping to others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure by them.
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by leavings,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down.
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruths,
and having drunk water— even if already pure— one who is about to study should sip water (perform ācamana).
The entire rule for purification and likewise the cleansing of objects has been declared to you for all castes; now learn the duties of women.
Neither by a girl, nor by a young woman, nor even by an aged woman should any action whatsoever be undertaken independently, even within the home.
In childhood, she should remain under the authority of her father; in youth, under that of her husband;
and when her husband has died, under that of her sons. A woman must never enjoy independence.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or her sons; for by such separation, she brings reproach upon both families.
She should always remain cheerful, be skillful in household duties, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in her expenditures.
To whomsoever her father or her brother— by the father's consent— may give her,
she should serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him.
For their sake, at the wedding, auspicious rites, benedictions, and sacrifices to Prajāpati are performed;
however, the formal giving away of the bride is the cause of the husband's ownership.
A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with mantras is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next, whether she is in her season or not.
Whether he is devoid of virtue, addicted to sensual pleasures, or destitute of good qualities,
a husband must always be attended upon by a virtuous wife like a god.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, whether he be living or dead, should never do anything displeasing to him who took her hand in marriage.
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but once her husband has died, she must not even utter the name of another man.
Until death, she should remain patient, self-controlled, and devoted to the celibate life,
longing for that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband.
Many thousands of Brahmins who remained celibate from their youth have gone to heaven without having established a lineage for their family.
When her husband has died, a virtuous wife who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who practice lifelong celibacy.
But that woman who, out of greed for her offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
No offspring born here belongs to anyone other than the biological father, nor does it belong to another's possession;
for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed.
She who, having abandoned her own husband though he be inferior, resorts to one who is superior, becomes censurable in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband. (Manu Smṛti 5.163)
But through infidelity with her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
She who does not deceive her husband through thought, word, or deed attains the world of her husband; she is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains supreme fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.
A twice-born man who knows the law should have his wife— who is of the same caste, of virtuous conduct, and who dies before him— cremated with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial implements.
Having given the sacred fires to his wife who has died before him during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the ceremony of taking a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
Following this rule, he should never neglect the five great sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of his life.
Having thus remained in the householder stage according to the rules, the twice-born who has completed his studies,
having subdued his senses, should dwell in the forest, self-restrained and in accordance with the law.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair,
and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should resort to the forest.
Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
Taking with him the *agnihotra* fire and the implements for the domestic fire,
he should depart from the village for the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should wear either a hide or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, a beard, and long nails.
From whatever food he may have, he should give an offering and alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
he should always be a giver and never a taker, showing compassion toward all living beings.
And he should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice pertaining to the three sacred fires according to the rule,
not omitting the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices through the practice of yoga.
He should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dakṣāyaṇa, in their proper sequence.

He should separately prepare sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and cooked rice offerings (caru), according to the rules, using pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons.
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots,
and fruits produced from pure trees, along with oils derived from fruits.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleśmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored,
as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a ploughshare, even if it has been discarded by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots and fruits grown within a village.
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may be one who washes away his impurities immediately, or one who stores food for a month;
he may store for six months, or even for a year.
Having procured food according to his ability, he should eat it either at night or during the day;
or he may eat only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime.
Or he may pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he may eat boiled barley-gruel only once.
Or, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in their season and fallen of their own accord.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the three ritual libations.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.
Performing ablutions at the three daily sessions, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more intense austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, observing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, having no sense of ownership toward shelters, and making his dwelling at the foot of a tree; Mn 6.26.
He should obtain alms sufficient for his journey from ascetic Brahmins alone,
or from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from the village,
receiving them either in the hollow of his hands, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd.
Living in the forest, a Brahmin should practice these and other initiations,
as well as various Upanishadic scriptures, for the sake of perfecting the self.
These [hermitages] are frequented by sages and brahmins who are householders,
for the sake of increasing their knowledge and austerity and for the purification of the body.
Or, having taken his stand upon the Aparājitā [direction], he should proceed straight toward that quarter,
disciplined, subsisting on water and air, until the fall of his body.
Having cast off his body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by alms and offerings, he who renounces increases after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of his ability, he should fix his mind on liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may depart from his home to the life of a wandering mendicant.
For him who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, goes forth from his home,
there are worlds consisting of splendor, O teacher of Brahman.
Since not even the slightest fear arises from living beings toward the twice-born,
there is no fear from any quarter for him who is liberated from the body.
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by sacred observances,
should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him.
One should always wander alone, without companions, for the sake of attaining perfection;
seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons it nor is he abandoned by it.
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food;
indifferent, free from agitation, a sage whose mind is absorbed in the Supreme Being.
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged garments, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, relying upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to external objects, and free from worldly desires,
he who seeks happiness should wander here with the self alone as his companion.
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by giving instructions or by engaging in discourse.
He should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants.
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly, self-restrained, without causing pain to any living beings.
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups in a sacrifice.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared to be the vessels for ascetics.
He should go for alms only once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached to sense-objects as well.

A mendicant should always go for alms when the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed.
He should not be dejected when he gains nothing, nor should he rejoice when he gains something;
he should take only what is necessary for the journey of life, remaining free from attachment to material possessions.
But one should utterly detest gains obtained through being honored;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through being honored.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should restrain the senses when they are being carried away by the objects of the senses.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
He should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
Separation from those who are dear, as well as union with those who are not dear, being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases; Mn 6.62.
He perceives the departure of this inner self from the body, its rebirth in a womb,
and its wanderings through thousands of millions of wombs.
The connection with suffering for embodied beings arises from unrighteousness,
while the inexhaustible union with happiness arises from righteousness and purposeful action.
And by means of yoga, he should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.
Even if he is corrupted, one should practice dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) he may be in;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of dharma.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (Manu Smṛti 6.67)
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk upon the earth after carefully scanning it, even when his body is exhausted.
Whatever living beings an ascetic may unintentionally harm by day or by night,
for the sake of purifying himself from those acts, he should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) after bathing.
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), when performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa and joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath.
One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
Through the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the course of this inner self among beings of high and low status— a course difficult to understand for those who have not disciplined themselves.
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of such vision enters the cycle of transmigration.
By means of non-violence, detachment of the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the rigorous practice of austerities, they attain that state in this world.
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent.
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so too one who abandons this body is liberated from the crocodile of suffering.
Having cast off his good deeds toward those dear to him and his evil deeds toward those who are not dear,
through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition,
then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments and being liberated from all pairs of opposites, he abides in Brahman alone.
All this that has been described here is indeed based on meditation;
for no one who is not self-knowing (anadhyātmavid) enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
He should constantly mutter the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and whatever is declared in the Vedānta.
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this very same is for those who possess knowledge.
This is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking the infinite.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant according to this sequential method,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
And among all these [orders], according to the injunctions of the Vedas and the Smṛtis,
the householder is said to be the best, for he supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their support in the householder.
Moreover, this tenfold dharma must be practiced with diligent effort at all times by the twice-born belonging to any of these four stages of life.
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-control, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma.
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma and,
having studied them, live according to them, attain the supreme goal.
Having practiced the Dharma characterized by the ten marks with a concentrated mind,
and having heard the Vedānta according to the rule, the twice-born man, freed from his debts, should renounce the world.
Having renounced all ritual acts and cast off the defects of action,
he should live happily under the sovereignty of his sons, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from desire,
he destroys his sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
This fourfold duty of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you;
it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the duty of kings.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin came about, and how he may attain supreme success.
A Kṣatriya who has duly received the Vedic consecration must,
according to the law, provide protection for all this [world].
For in this world without a king, people would have fled in fear from every side;
therefore, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this.
Having extracted the eternal constituent parts of Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; of Agni and Varuṇa; and of Candra and Vitteśa.
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in his splendor.
Like the sun, he dazzles both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look upon him directly.
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama);
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and the great Indra.
A king must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking "he is merely a human being";
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form. (Mn 7.8)
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it incautiously;
but the fire of a king's wrath consumes the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
Having duly considered the task at hand, his own power, and the place and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-born Śrī, in whose prowess victory, and in whose anger death; for he is composed of all splendor.
But whoever hates him out of delusion perishes without a doubt;
for the king sets his mind quickly upon his destruction.
Therefore, that king should apply the law toward those he favors,
and he should not deviate from that law even toward those he disfavors.
For its sake, the Lord formerly created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, provide for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties.
Having duly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of those men],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
The rod governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be the law (dharma).
When properly supported after careful deliberation, he pleases all his subjects;
but when administered without due deliberation, he causes destruction on every side.
If the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and likewise a dog might lick the oblation (havis);
there would be no sense of ownership in anything, and the lower would prevail over the higher.
The whole world is subdued by punishment, for a pure man is hard to find;
indeed, out of fear of punishment, the entire world is fit for the enjoyment of life.
Even gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds,
and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when they are oppressed by punishment alone.
All social classes would become corrupted, all boundaries would be broken, and there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment. (Manu 7.24)
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks about, destroying evil,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who should be appointed as its administrator.
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by that very punishment.
For punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul;
it destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen if he deviates from righteousness.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.
He cannot be led by the right path by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect, and attached to sensual objects. (Manu Smṛti 7.30)
Punishment can be effectively administered by one who is pure, true to his word, follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies,
straightforward toward friends, and full of forbearance toward Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
But for a king who acts in the opposite manner and has not conquered himself,
his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are each established in their respective duties, in due order.
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his servants,
all that I shall declare to you duly and in proper sequence.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon Brahmins who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.
One should always serve aged Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
From them, even one who is already self-disciplined should constantly learn the principles of discipline;
for a king who is self-disciplined never comes to ruin.
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those dwelling in the forest have attained kingdoms through discipline.
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (Mn 7.41)
Pṛthu obtained the kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple Vedic knowledge, the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti),
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the science of the self, and the practical applications of the economic arts from the people.
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control.
One should diligently avoid these ten calamities arising from desire, as well as those eight born of anger, which have miserable endings.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma, but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of them by his very self.
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the three types of performance arts, and idle wandering— this is the tenfold group born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault with others' merits, and the harshness of speech and punishment—this group of eight arises from anger. (Manu Smṛti 7.48)
One should strive with effort to conquer greed, which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these groups arise from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— one should know that this group of four, in their respective order, is the most grievous among the set arising from desire.
One should know that this triad— inflicting physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the misappropriation of property— is always grievous, even within the group of offenses born of anger.
A self-possessed man should know that among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more serious than the one following it.
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
the man of calamities sinks lower and lower, while the man free from calamities goes to heaven when he dies.
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone to accomplish, especially so without assistance; how much more so is a kingdom of great consequence?
With them, he should constantly deliberate upon common matters:
peace and war, stability, acquisition, protection, and the consolidation of what has been gained.
Having ascertained their respective individual intentions,
he should act for his own welfare in matters concerning all of them collectively.
But the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his ministers.
Having placed constant trust in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he may then undertake his work.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.
He should appoint as many vigilant, skillful, and discerning men as are required for the performance of his duties.
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in the workshops;
and those who are pure and timid within the inner apartments.
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and conduct, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.
A messenger who is loyal, pure, skillful, mindful, knowledgeable of place and time, handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised by kings.

The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of discipline rests with the power of punishment; the treasury and the kingdom rest with the king; and peace and its opposite rest with the envoy.
For it is the messenger indeed who unites those who are divided and also divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated from one another.

Through secret hints, gestures, and movements, he should discern the king's facial expression, his hints, and his actions, as well as what he intends to do regarding his undertakings and toward his servants.
Having understood in its true essence everything intended by the enemy king,
he should apply such effort as will not cause harm to himself.
He should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by Āryas, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive neighbors, and providing a means of livelihood.
Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort, he should dwell in a city.
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Of these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, burrow-dwellers, and aquatic creatures;
the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, human beings, and gods.
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress,
so too do foes not injure a king who has taken shelter in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight off a hundred; a hundred can fight off ten thousand; therefore, a fortress is established.
That [fortress] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
it should also be provided with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
In the center of that [plot], he should have his own house constructed—
secure, suitable for all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue.
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.
The king should perform various sacrifices accompanied by liberal sacrificial fees,
and for the sake of righteousness, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins.
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trusted agents;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects as toward his own father.
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men engaged in their work.
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this is declared to be the inexhaustible Brāhma treasury of kings.
Neither thieves nor enemies can steal it, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brāhmaṇas.
It overflows not, it does not fail, and it never perishes;
an offering made into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward; to one who has studied the Vedas, it yields a hundred-thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields an infinite reward.
Indeed, depending on the excellence of the recipient and the degree of one's own faith,
one enjoys the fruit of a gift— whether small or great— after death.
Whatever substance is given with faith to a worthy recipient, according to the rules regarding place and time, that is the means for accomplishing dharma.
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior while protecting his subjects,
the king, mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya, must not retreat from battle.
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to the Brahmins are the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
In battles, kings who, desiring to slay one another,
fight with their utmost strength and do not turn their backs, go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with barbed arrows, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are ablaze with fire.
One should not strike one who has climbed onto dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with joined palms;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."

One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should not strike one who is suffering from the loss of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away.
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies,
incurs all whatever evil deeds his master has committed.
Moreover, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter,
the master takes all of that from one who is killed while retreating.
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, cattle, women,
all types of property, and base metals— whatever one conquers belongs to him.
And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually.
This eternal warrior-dharma has been declared as unadorned;
a Kṣatriya, while slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.
One should seek to obtain what has not been obtained, guard with effort what has been obtained,
increase what has been guarded, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should know that these four types are the means for achieving the goals of human existence;
one should perform their practice constantly and correctly, without indolence.
One should seek what has not been obtained by means of force; protect what has been obtained with vigilance;
increase what has been protected through growth; and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment uplifted, always display his manly prowess, always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds the rod of punishment uplifted;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod.
He should always conduct himself without guile and never with guile;
being ever well-restrained, he should also recognize the guile employed by his enemies.
Let not another know his own weakness, but let him know the weakness of others;
he should hide his own limbs like a tortoise and guard his own vulnerability.
Like a crane, he should contemplate his goals; like a lion, he should exert his prowess;
like a wolf, he should snatch his prey; and like a hare, he should flee.
While he is thus victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation.
If, however, they do not abide by those [means], he should gradually bring them under control by force alone, using the first three expedients.
Among the four means of policy, conciliation and the others, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom.
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
The king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, oppresses his own kingdom,
shall soon be deprived both of his realm and his life, along with his kinsmen.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
He should always carry out this regulation for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness.
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom.
He should appoint a lord over a village, likewise a lord over ten villages,
a lord over twenty, a lord over a hundred, and also a lord over a thousand.
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults that have arisen in the village to the leader of ten villages;
the leader of ten should report them to the leader of twenty.
The lord of twenty, however, shall report all that to the lord of a hundred;
and the lord of a hundred villages shall himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Whatever is to be paid daily by the village-dwellers to the king,
such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth, the village headman (grāmika) shall receive those.

The collector of ten should enjoy the produce of one family, the collector of twenty that of five families; the superintendent of a hundred villages should enjoy a village, and the lord of a thousand a city.
Indeed, another minister of the king, who is affectionate and vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their private matters.
And in every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a prominent place and of formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.
He himself should always supervise them all personally,
and he should correctly ascertain their conduct in the realms through spies.
For the king's protectors are generally servants who seize the property of others and are deceitful; he must guard these subjects from them.
Those of evil intent who seize wealth solely from litigants,
the king should confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment.
The king should daily provide maintenance and a place of residence, according to their respective duties, for women and servants who are engaged in his service.
A paṇa should be given as the daily wage for the lowest servant, and six paṇas for the highest;
likewise, clothing should be provided every six months, and one droṇa of grain every month.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of the goods, the king should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants.
Having considered how both the king and the doer of actions may be joined with their respective fruits,
the king should always determine the taxes in his realm accordingly.
Just as water-creatures, young calves, and bees consume their food little by little,
so should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is small and small.
The king shall take one-fiftieth of cattle and gold;
and one-eighth, one-sixth, or even one-twelfth of the grain.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
And of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and wickerwork;
of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone.
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his realm perish from hunger.
In whosever kingdom a learned Śrotriya perishes from hunger,
his kingdom likewise shall perish from hunger before long.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son.
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
The king should cause even the common people in his realm who live by trade to pay some small amount known as a tax for the year.
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month.
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one would surely afflict both oneself and them.
The lord of the earth should be both harsh and mild after considering the task at hand;
indeed, O King, he who is both harsh and mild becomes esteemed by all.
When weary from supervising the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the law, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Having thus performed all these duties pertaining to himself,
he should protect these subjects, remaining both disciplined and vigilant.
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—
even though he looks on with his servants— he is dead, not alive.
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed rewards is joined with righteousness.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications with a concentrated mind,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with words of blessing;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended to a mountain ridge, or having gone to a secluded spot in a temple,
or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate on counsel unobserved.
That king who, even if devoid of treasury, enjoys the entire earth while common folk do not discover his secret counsel, [is truly successful]. (MN 7.148 [149M])
At the time of reciting the mantra, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, animals, the very aged, women, barbarians, the diseased, and the deformed.
Those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, disclose a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue,
he should reflect upon dharma, pleasure, and wealth, either alone or together with them.
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons; Mn 7.152 [153M]
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining tasks,
the conduct within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
He should also truly understand in their entirety the eightfold business, the five classes [of spies],
the loyalty and disloyalty [of his subjects], and the conduct of the circle of states.
He should diligently ascertain the conduct of the middle king, the activities of one who desires to conquer, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy.
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle [of states];
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
The five others are known as ministers, the kingdom, fortresses, wealth, and the army;
each of these has been described briefly, making seventy-two in total.
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the one who serves the enemy;
immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party.
He should win them all over by means of conciliation and other such measures,
whether employed individually or collectively, through personal prowess and through statesmanship.
He should always consider the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.
Having carefully considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment, marching, making peace, waging war, double-dealing, or seeking refuge. (Manu 7.161)
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds;
likewise, marching and encamping are each twofold, and seeking protection is recorded as being of two types.
When the undertaking of the journey is common, as well as when it is the opposite,
then that peace treaty should be known as having two characteristics and being connected with the future.
War is declared to be of two kinds: that undertaken by oneself for the sake of accomplishing a task, whether at the proper time or not, and that waged against a friend who has done one harm.
When an urgent matter has arisen by chance,
marching alone or in alliance with a friend— these two types of marching are prescribed.
When one's own power has gradually diminished due to fate or past actions,
or out of consideration for a friend, neutrality is declared to be of two kinds.
The maintenance of both the army and the master for the sake of accomplishing the objective is declared to be of two kinds as "duplicity" by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy.
Seeking refuge with the virtuous for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose when oppressed by enemies is considered to be of two kinds.
When he perceives that his own superiority in the future is certain,
while the suffering in the present is slight, then he should resort to peace.
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased,
and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war.
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit,
and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is depleted of both mounts and troops,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.
When the king considers his enemy to be in every way more powerful,
he should then divide his army into two parts and accomplish his own purpose.
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of his enemies,
then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king.
One should always serve with all efforts like a teacher that king who effects the suppression of both his subjects and the enemy's forces.
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from taking refuge [in such a king],
he should nevertheless engage in a fair fight there without hesitation.
A king who knows the principles of policy should employ every means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him.
He should examine all future undertakings and their immediate consequences,
as well as the merits and defects of all past actions according to their true nature.
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who understands the consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies.
He should arrange everything in such a way that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.
Then the lord, when setting out against the enemy's kingdom,
should march slowly toward the enemy's city according to this following procedure.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
or else in the months of Phālguna or Caitra, the lord of the earth may set out on his expedition according to his strength.
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for his enemy.
Having performed the ritual at the root [of the tree] and the journey-related rites according to rule, and having secured a dwelling and properly stationed spies; Mn 7.184 [185M]
Having cleared the three types of roads and his own sixfold forces according to the rules for a prolonged campaign,
he should march toward the enemy's city.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a hidden enemy who has become a friend, as well as one who has gone away and returned; for such a person is the most dangerous of foes.
He should march along that road in the staff-array, or the wagon-array,
or the boar-array, the crocodile-array, the needle-array, or the eagle-array.
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, in that direction he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus formation.
The commander-in-chief and the general shall station their forces in all directions;
and from whichever direction he apprehends danger, he should designate that as the "east."
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—
men who are skilled in both their positions and in battle, fearless, and incorruptible.
One should make a small number of troops fight in close formation, but one may extend a large number at will;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should make them fight.

One should fight on level ground with chariots and horses; likewise, one should fight on marshy ground with boats and elephants; and in terrain covered by trees and shrubs, or on open ground, one should fight with bows, swords, shields, and other weapons.
He should station men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena,
as well as those who are tall and those who are short, at the vanguard of the army.
Having arrayed his army, he should gladden it and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the gestures of the enemies as they engage in combat.
Having besieged his enemy, he should remain there and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly spoil his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel.
He should break down tanks as well as walls and moats;
he should launch a sudden assault upon him at night and likewise terrify him.
He should instigate those who can be sown with discord, and he should remain aware of their actions;
when fate is favorable, he should fight, free from fear and desiring victory.
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension— either collectively or individually— and never by means of war.
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two combatants,
and defeat likewise in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
When even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible,
he should fight in such a manner that, being well-equipped, he may conquer his enemies.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties.
But having understood the intended purpose of all these [claimants] in brief,
he should install there a member of that same lineage and establish a formal covenant.
And he should establish authorities for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and he should honor him with jewels, together with the principal men.
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving causes pleasure;
at the proper time, the practice of bestowing desired objects is highly praised.
All this action is dependent upon the two ordinances, the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, but in the human there exists the possibility of action.
When human effort is joined with destiny,
it proceeds toward the accomplishment of its purpose through great hardship.
Even when joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort,
the field yields fruit only through human effort.
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water,
are brought about here through destiny and through human effort with diligence.
Or he may march together with him, having diligently made a treaty,
while keeping in view the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and the ally in the circle of states,
one should obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy.
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend, even if that friend is currently weak, provided he is capable of enduring for the future.
One who knows the Dharma, is grateful, and is naturally contented;
one who is devoted, steadfast in his undertakings—such a light friend is highly praised.
The wise declare it a hardship to have for an enemy one who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and resolute.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, compassion, magnanimity, and the constant arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial; Mn 7.211 [215M]
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for his own sake.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together,
the wise man should employ every means, both those that are combined and those that are separate.
Relying upon these three— the seeker, the goal to be sought, and all means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
after exercising and bathing, shall enter the inner apartments at midday to eat.
There, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be subverted, and who have neutralized poison with mantras.
He should employ all substances that counteract poison as antidotes, and,
remaining self-controlled, he should always wear gems that destroy poison.
And women who have been examined, whose dress and ornaments are pure, and who are composed, should touch him with fans, water, and incense.
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food,
as well as in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the appropriate time, he should again attend to his duties.
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the military personnel once more,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, while bearing his weapon, listen within his inner apartments to the reports of those who reveal secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating.
Having eaten there a little more, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to bed at the proper time and rise free from fatigue.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
But when the king desires to examine legal cases, he should enter the court modestly, accompanied by Brahmins as well as ministers who are experts in counsel.
Seated there, or even standing, having raised his right hand and being modest in dress and ornaments, he shall look into the legal affairs of the litigants.
Every day, they shall record separately, according to the eighteen titles of law, the causes of dispute as perceived by local custom and as prescribed by the scriptures.
