Of these, the first is the non-payment of debts, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given. (Manu 8.4)
The non-payment of wages, the breach of a contract, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and a herdsman; Mn 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault, theft, violence (sāhasa), and the abduction of women; Mn 8.6.
The duties of women and men, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these are the eighteen titles of law established here in this world.
In these matters, the king should decide the legal cases of men who are mostly engaged in disputes, by relying upon the eternal Dharma.
But when the king himself does not personally attend to the inspection of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to inspect those cases.
Surrounded by three members of the court, he should examine his judicial duties,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together,
along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly to be a court of Brahmā.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (Manu 8.12)
One should either not enter the assembly or speak what is just;
for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner.
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain. (Manu 8.14)
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, one must not violate Dharma, lest violated Dharma destroy us.
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed a bull (vṛṣa); the gods know him who treats that Dharma with contempt as a "vṛṣala" (outcaste). Therefore, one should not let Dharma perish.
Dharma alone is the true friend that follows one even in death;
for everything else indeed perishes along with the body.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes [sinless], and the members of the assembly are released from guilt;
the sin goes to the perpetrator where one who deserves censure is censured. (Manu 8.19)
One who merely lives by his birth may, if he so desires, be called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇabruva) as the expounder of dharma to the king; but a Śūdra must never be so under any circumstances.
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow in the mud, even as he looks on.
That kingdom which consists mostly of Śūdras, which is overrun by atheists, and which is devoid of the twice-born,
quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease.
Having occupied the seat of justice, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.
Having understood both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, eyes, and movements.
The internal mind is apprehended through outward forms, gestures, gait, movements, speech, and the expressions of the eyes and face.
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his minority.
The same protection should be afforded to the daughters of barren women,
to those whose families have perished, to women devoted to their husbands, to widows, and to those who are afflicted by illness.
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still living,
a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the penalty prescribed for thieves.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that period, the king shall take it.
He who says "this is mine" shall be examined according to the rule;
having verified the form, number, and other characteristics, the owner deserves that property.
One who reports the place and time of a lost object accurately,
as well as its color, form, and size, deserves a fine equal to that [stolen] object.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king may take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of property lost and then found.
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves who may be caught therein, the king shall have them executed by means of an elephant.
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth part or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth,
or a smaller fraction of the value of that very deposit.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the lord of all.
But whatever ancient treasure a king may discover buried in the earth,
he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury.
For the king is the lord of the earth; as such, he receives a half-share from the protection of ancient treasures and minerals found in the ground. (Manu 8.39)
The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, shall establish the specific duty for each individual.
Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world.
Neither the king himself nor his official should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought before him by another.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood,
so should a king trace the path of dharma by means of inference.
Abiding by the rules of legal procedure, he should examine the truth, the matter at hand, himself, the witnesses, the place, the appearance, and the time.

Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, that one should establish as the law for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not inconsistent with the sacred tradition.
When urged by a creditor for the purpose of recovering the debt of a debtor,
the king shall cause the creditor to receive from the debtor the amount of wealth that has been proven.
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own property,
by those very means he should compel the debtor to pay, having first won him over.
One should recover a debt through legal process, through trickery, through customary practice,
and by force as the fifth means.
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own.
But if one denies the debt, yet it is proven by evidence,
the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor's claim and a small fine according to his ability.
When the debtor denies the debt in an assembly after being told "Pay!",
the plaintiff must point out the person who can testify, or he shall specify another means of proof.
He who points out what should not be pointed out, he who denies after having pointed it out, and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows; Mn 8.53.
Furthermore, he who, having stated what was to be stated, subsequently retracts it;
and he who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly proposed.
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when a question is being put to him, and he who runs away; Mn 8.55.

If, when told "speak," he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said, or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that account. (Manu 8.56)
If one says, "I have witnesses," but when told "Produce them," fails to produce them,
the judge should declare him also defeated on these grounds.

If the plaintiff does not speak within three fortnights, he should be bound and punished according to the law; if he does not state his case within that time, he is defeated in accordance with justice.
If a person conceals an object to whatever extent, or if he speaks falsely regarding its value to whatever extent,
both of them, being ignorant of the law, shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth while remaining steadfast, denies the charge,
must be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be employed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them.

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, are fit to give testimony when summoned for the sake of wealth; but no others whatsoever are so fit, except in times of emergency.

Trustworthy persons from all castes should be appointed as witnesses in legal matters, provided they are knowledgeable in all dharmas and free from greed; however, one should avoid those who possess the opposite qualities.
One should not appoint as witnesses those who have a financial interest in the matter, nor friends, nor enemies,
nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt.
The king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is mute, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an aged man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane, nor oppressed by hunger or thirst;
neither one afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by passion, nor angry, nor even a thief [should be questioned].
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; and virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras, while those of low birth shall testify for those of low origin.
But whoever, being a witness to the facts, should give testimony for litigants within a house, in a forest, or even in the event of a threat to life; Mn_8.69.
In the absence of a woman, the business may be conducted by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick who give false testimony is unstable, as is the speech of those whose minds are agitated.
In all cases of violence, in theft and adultery,
and in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, the king should accept the majority; but if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.
Testimony is established by seeing or hearing in person;
in that case, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from merit or wealth.
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men concerning anything other than what was seen or heard goes headfirst to hell after death and is excluded from heaven.
Even where one has not been formally appointed, if one should see or hear anything,
even when questioned there, one should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but even many women shall not;
for the intellect of women is unsteady, and others as well who are tainted by defects [are inadmissible].
Whatever they may say in accordance with their own nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is useless.
When the witnesses have arrived in the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant,
the judge shall interrogate them, consoling them with this following procedure.
Whatever you two know of each other's mutual conduct regarding this matter, declare it all in truth; for your role here is that of witnesses.
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking falsehood in testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
By truth a witness is purified; by truth dharma increases.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
Evil-doers think, "No one sees us";
yet the gods see them, as does their own inner self.
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, the wind, night,
the two twilights, and Dharma are the witnesses to the conduct of all embodied beings.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either the north or the east.
One should question a Brāhmaṇa with "Speak! a Kṣatriya with "Speak the truth!
a Vaiśya with "By means of cattle, grain, and gold," and a Śūdra with all the [names of] heinous crimes.
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, for those who kill women or children,
for the betrayer of friends, and for the ungrateful— those same worlds shall befall him who speaks falsely.
O gentle one, whatever merit you have acquired since birth—all that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise. (Manu 8.90)
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and sin stands eternally within your heart.
If you have no dispute with that god Yama Vaivasvata who resides within your heart, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, and carrying a skull-bowl, begging for alms while tormented by hunger and thirst,
blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy.
He who, when questioned during a legal determination, should give a false answer, shall go headlong into the darkness of hell as a sinner. (Manu 8.94)
That man who, having entered an assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts or what he has not personally witnessed, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man.
For the gods know no other person in this world to be superior to that learned man whose inner self (kṣetrajña) does not harbor suspicion when he speaks.
Hear now, O gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen a man destroys by speaking falsely when giving testimony in a court of law.
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men.
By speaking a falsehood for the sake of gold, one destroys both those who are born and those yet unborn;
by a falsehood regarding land, one destroys everything. Therefore, do not speak a falsehood concerning land.
They say that [the law of] land applies to water, to the enjoyment of women and sexual intercourse,
to aquatic gems, and to all things made of stone.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen.
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, traders, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers as one would Śūdras.
When a man speaks thus regarding legal matters, even though he knows otherwise, he does not fall from heaven; they call that the speech of the gods.
In a case where the death penalty would otherwise be pronounced for a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa, a falsehood should be spoken; for that is superior to the truth.
And they should worship Sarasvatī with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to Vāk and Gaṇeśa,
effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood.
Or he may offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses addressed to the Waters.
If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth on the whole amount.
If, within seven days of the testimony having been given,
a witness suffers from disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.
But in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot ascertain the truth in its true nature, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.
Oaths have been taken for the sake of a legal purpose by great seers and by gods;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before the king, the son of Pijavana.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, he perishes both in this world and after death.
In matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cattle, fuel,
and in coming to the aid of a Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin in taking an oath.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by [the truth of] the Vedas, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins.
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should have him touch the heads of his wife and children individually.
He whom the kindled fire does not burn, whom the waters do not cause to float up,
and who does not quickly meet with misfortune— such a person should be known as pure in his oath.
For in ancient times, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother,
the fire— the watcher of the world— did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness.
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; what has been done shall be as if undone.
Testimony is declared to be false when given out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger, as well as from ignorance or childishness.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any one of these cases.
For taking [property] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first amercement;
for out of fear, two middle amercements; and for out of friendship, four times the first amercement.
From lust, the first [penalty] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold;
from ignorance, it is two full hundred; but from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony to be for the purpose of ensuring that dharma does not deviate and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
A righteous king, having punished them with a fine, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony; however, he shall only exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment which may be applied to the three social orders; however, a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and fifthly the feet;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered the strength of the offender and the gravity of the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys reputation and ruins fame;
it also prevents one from attaining heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, and immediately after that, the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and beyond that, the punishment of corporal death.
But when he is unable to restrain them even by execution,
then he may employ all these four means against them.
I shall fully declare all those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are established on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the *trasareṇu*, the first among the measures of weight.
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in measure;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those [rājasarṣapas] are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium-sized barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together should be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or a *paṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure as being equal to four *sauvarṇikas*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest.
When a debt that is due has been admitted, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, the fine is double that—such is the ordinance of Manu.
A moneylender may stipulate the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Recalling the duty of the virtuous, he may take two percent;
for by taking two percent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth.
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five,
or ten percent per month, respectively, according to the order of the social classes.
But one shall not obtain interest on a secured loan if it is used for the benefit [of the debtor];
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
Both an open deposit and a sealed deposit ought not to suffer from the lapse of time;
if they remain for a long duration, both shall be liable to forfeiture.
Cattle, camels, draft horses, and those horses being used for training, when enjoyed with mutual consent, never perish [as a debt]. (Manu 8.146)
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he is not entitled to recover it.

If the owner is not an idiot and is not a minor, and yet the property is enjoyed by another in his presence, that possession is subverted by the legal proceeding; the enjoyer deserves to forfeit that property.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property,
and the property of a Vedic scholar are not lost through adverse possession.
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must forfeit half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
in the case of grain, fruit, wool, or beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.
An interest exceeding the legal rate, or one that is excessive, is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for [the law] permits only five percent per month.

One should not take interest exceeding that for a year, nor that which is not sanctioned; likewise, one should not take compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, or bodily interest.
He who, being unable to pay the debt, wishes to enter into a new transaction, shall,
after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond.
Without producing the gold, he may exchange it for other goods;
he ought to pay back as much interest as has accrued.
One who has entered upon the increase of his capital and is established according to the rules of place and time will not obtain that fruit if he disregards place and time.
Those skilled in sea voyages, who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose, establish whatever rate of interest; that shall be the rate for the recovery of the loan in that case.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
he shall pay the debt from his own property to that person if he fails to produce him.
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous gift, what is owed for gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
if the surety for payment dies, the king shall cause even the heirs to pay.
Furthermore, when the debtor does not pay, the creditor may seek the debt from the surety, provided the nature of the obligation is well known;
but if the surety dies afterwards, by what means could he seek it? (Mn 8.161)
But if the surety has been designated as having sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who has been designated.
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, or dependent, or by a child, or by an elderly person, or one that is not binding, is not valid.
Even if a statement is well-established, it does not constitute truth if it is spoken externally regarding matters that are merely conventional and worldly. (Manu Smṛti 8.164)
Whatever is mortgaged or sold through fraud, whatever gift or acceptance of a gift is obtained through fraud,
or wherever one perceives deceit— let him annul all that.
If the borrower should perish after having incurred an expenditure for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by his kinsmen, even if they are divided from him.
Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it.
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—
Manu has declared all transactions effected by force to be null and void."
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
four, however, prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.
A king, even when impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death.
From the enjoyment [of taxes], from the blending of castes, and from the protection of the weak, the strength of the king arises; he prospers both in this world and after death.

Therefore, like Yama himself, the king should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, having conquered his anger and subdued his senses.
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs unjustly,
his enemies will soon bring him under their control.
But he who, having restrained both desire and anger, views all matters according to dharma,
his subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean.

He who reports to the king a creditor who is recovering his debt by his own will shall be made by the king to pay one-fourth of that amount as a fine, and the debt itself shall be paid to the creditor.
A debtor should repay the creditor in equal value even by means of labor;
one of equal or lower caste may do so, but one of higher caste should pay that back gradually.
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of justice those legal matters of disputing men that are established by the evidence of witnesses.
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in the Dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable.
Whatever object a man deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt.
When one who has been asked for a deposit does not return it to the depositor,
he shall be questioned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with trustworthy persons endowed with age and physical appearance, and by means of pretexts; Mn 8.182.
If he should restore it exactly as it was deposited and in the same condition as it was made,
there exists therein nothing for which he may be prosecuted by others.
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he should be seized by both parties and compelled to pay; such is the established principle of the law.
A sealed deposit and an open deposit must never be handed over to a next-of-kin;
these two perish if [the owner] perishes, but they do not perish if he does not perish.
But if one should personally deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
He should seek that object with honesty and in a friendly manner;
or, having investigated the man's conduct, he should settle the matter through conciliation alone.
In all these cases of deposits, this same rule shall apply for their recovery;
however, in the case of an ocean-deposit, one shall not recover anything if the depositary does not bring it back from there.
If it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire,
he need not pay for it, provided that he did not take anything from it himself.
One should seek out, by every possible means and even by Vedic oaths, both the one who misappropriates a deposit and the one who did not actually entrust it.
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having made a deposit—
both of these should be punished like thieves, or compelled to pay a fine equal to the value of the object.
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value;
likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit (upanidhi), without distinction.
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should seize the property of another,
must be put to death publicly with various modes of execution along with his accomplices.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; he who declares otherwise deserves punishment.
If a gift has been made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the gift was given, so it should be taken back.
In such cases, the king shall make a decision regarding deposited wealth as well as that which has been entrusted out of friendship, without causing loss to the holder of the deposit.
One who sells another's property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, should not be made a witness; he is a thief who considers himself no thief.
He shall be compelled to pay a fine of six hundred panas along with his family;
if he has no family and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
But that gift or sale which is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
Where enjoyment is seen but no source [of ownership] is seen anywhere, there the source is the cause, and not the mere enjoyment; such is the settled rule.
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of a family assembly,
he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified.

Now, if the seller cannot produce the original source of the goods and has cleared himself by proving a public purchase, he shall not be punished by the king and is released; the owner of the lost property recovers his wealth.
An object whose form has been mixed with another is not fit for sale,
nor is that which is worthless, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is concealed at a distance.
"If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom, he may marry both for the price of a single dowary; so Manu has declared."

A giver does not deserve punishment if he has previously declared the defects [of the girl], provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already had sexual intercourse. Mn 8.205.
If an officiating priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty,
a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the co-performers.
And when the sacrificial fees have been given, if he causes his own work to be neglected,
he shall receive his entire share even if he has it performed by another.
In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, that person alone shall receive them; or alternatively, all [the officiants] may share them together.
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the kindling of the fires;
or the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Among all of them, the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part.
When men here join together to perform their respective duties,
the apportionment of their shares must be determined according to this rule.
If wealth has been given by someone to anyone who asks for it for the sake of dharma,
and if that wealth subsequently does not serve that purpose, it shall not have been properly given to him.
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed,
he shall be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft.
Thus has been declared the lawful manner of non-repayment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
If a hired servant, though not ill, fails out of pride to perform his work as prescribed,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid.
But one who was distressed and, having recovered his health, performs the work as originally stipulated from the beginning,
shall indeed receive that wage even after a long period of time.
As it has been said: "Whether he is distressed or healthy, if one does not have that work performed, his wages must not be paid, even if the work was only slightly incomplete. (Manu 8.217)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
If a man, having made a formal agreement with a village, a district, or a corporation,
should break it out of greed, the king shall banish him from the realm.
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the compact to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and a royal śatamāna.
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies.
If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have cause for regret,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.
But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause [the goods] to be given;
both he who takes them and he who gives them shall be fined six hundred by the king.
But for him who gives away a maiden who has defects without disclosing them,
the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas.
But that man who, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a virgin" without showing any fault in her, shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (Manu 8.225)
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are established for maidens alone;
they are never for non-maidens among men, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites.
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of wifehood;
their completion, however, should be recognized by the wise as occurring at the seventh step.
In whatever matter one may feel remorse after it has been done,
he should be established on the path of righteousness by this procedure.
I shall now fully declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the legal dispute concerning cattle arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen.
During the day, the responsibility for what must be said lies with the keeper; at night, it lies with the owner, provided [the animal] is in his house.
Otherwise, if the security of the property is otherwise compromised, the keeper shall incur the responsibility for what must be said.
A cowherd who is maintained with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; this shall be the wages for a herdsman if he receives no other pay.
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog,
or dies in a dangerous place due to a lack of human effort, the keeper alone shall make restitution.
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the keeper is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his master at the proper place and time.
Upon the death of animals, one should give the ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinews, and bile to the owners, and show them the branded marks.
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
if a wolf should forcibly kill one, the guilt for that shall fall upon the herdsman.
If, among those cows being kept together and grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
The common land around a village shall be one hundred bows on all sides, or three throws of a yoke-pin;
for a city, it shall be three times that amount.
If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there,
the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals.
One should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it,
and one should eliminate every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass.
On a path, in a field that is enclosed, or at the edge of a village, the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unattended.
But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
however, in all cases, it is the settled rule that a portion must be given to the owner of the field.
Manu has declared that a cow that has recently calved within ten days, bulls, and animals dedicated to the gods— whether they have a keeper or are unattended— are not subject to punishment.
In the event of a transgression by the owner of the field, the fine shall be ten times his share;
however, if it occurs through the ignorance of the servants, the fine for the owner of the field shall be half of that.
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule in cases of transgression involving owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and their keepers.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.
And he should plant boundary trees such as the nyagrodha, aśvattha, kiṃśuka, śālmalī,
sāla, tāla, and other milky-sap trees.
Bushes, various kinds of bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and plots of land,
as well as reeds and thickets of kubjaka shrubs— thus the boundary is not lost.
Ponds, wells, large tanks, and springs; Mn 8.248a.
And at the junctions of boundaries, he should establish works of public utility and temples for the deities.
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made concealed,
having observed that among men in this world there is constant confusion regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand; Mn 8.250.
And whatever objects of this kind the earth might swallow due to the passage of time,
he should cause them to be placed secretly at junctions and boundaries.
By these signs, the king should determine the boundary between two disputing parties,
as well as by continuous prior possession and by the flow of water.
If there were doubt even when the boundary marks are seen,
the decision in a dispute over boundaries would depend solely on the testimony of witnesses.
In the presence of the village families and the two litigants themselves, the witnesses must be questioned regarding the boundary marks along the border.
But having questioned them, he shall establish the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, recording the entire boundary and all of them by name.
Bearing the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and bound by their own good deeds, they shall lead you with justice.
Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
But in the absence of witnesses, four villagers residing on the borders shall, being purified,
determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
But in the absence of neighboring witnesses within the boundary of the original inhabitants, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests: Mn_8.259.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers; Mn 8.260.
But whatever those witnesses may say when questioned regarding the boundary marks at the junctions,
the king shall establish that according to the law for both villages.
The determination of boundaries for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be understood as depending upon the testimony of the neighbors. (Manu Smṛti 8.262)
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.
When a boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to some [parties] on account of their prior benefit; such is the settled rule.
Thus has the law regarding the determination of boundaries been declared in its entirety;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
in the case of a Vaiśya, the fine should be forty-five, and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
When members of the twice-born castes of equal rank commit an offense against one another, the fine shall be twelve [paṇas];
however, in cases where the dispute is not worthy of being spoken about, that same fine shall be doubled.
But one of low birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin.
But for one who utters their names or castes with malice,
a red-hot iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
If he gives instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins out of pride,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
One who, out of arrogance, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas.
Whether one is one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise similarly deformed,
even if speaking the truth, one should be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa.
One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher. (Manu 8.275)
A wise king should impose punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (Manu Smṛti 8.276)
In the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes,
the application of punishment shall be exactly as prescribed, with the exception of physical mutilation.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter I shall proclaim the legal determination concerning physical assault.
If a person of the lowest caste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu.
Raising his hand or his staff [in anger], he deserves the cutting off of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of that foot. (Mn 8.280)
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of a superior caste shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be gashed.
If one spits out of pride, the king shall cause both lips to be cut off;
if one urinates [upon him], the penis; and if one passes wind [against him], the anus.
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off both hands without hesitation;
likewise if they seize him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
In accordance with the degree of utility derived from all forest trees, so should punishment be inflicted for injury to them; such is the settled rule.
When an assault has been committed against humans or animals,
the king shall inflict a punishment that is proportionate to the severity of the suffering caused.
And for the crushing of a limb, as well as for wounds and bloodshed,
he shall be made to pay the expenses incurred in recovery or even the full fine.
If one should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king.
For leather goods, articles made of leather,
wood, or clay, as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
They say there are ten exemptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in any other case, a punishment is ordained.

When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction, or when there is a breakage of the axle or likewise of the wheel of the vehicle; Mn 8.291.
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a vehicle's harness, nor for its yoke or reins, nor when one cries out, "Get away! Mn 8.292.
If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas.
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the punishment;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas].
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
he should cause the death of living beings, the punishment in that case is not to be deliberated.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is immediate and equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, and horses, it is half [the penalty].
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
For killing donkeys, goats, or sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
but for killing a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother,
when they have committed an offense, may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But he must strike on the back of the body, and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, he incurs the guilt of a thief.
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase.
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is perpetually one in which the gift of fearlessness is the sacrificial fee.
A sixth part of all merit accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of the demerit accrues to him who fails to protect.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes a sharer of a sixth part of that through his proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices every day with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees.
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls,
a share of produce, and fines, shall immediately go to hell.
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part of their produce as tax,
is the one who carries away the entire impurity of all the world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, and one who fails to protect while consuming [the wealth of others], goes to a downward state.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrificial rites.
A lord who seeks his own welfare must always forgive litigants who revile him,
as well as children, the elderly, and the sick.
He who, when insulted by those in distress, endures it with patience, is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure it, goes to hell because of that.
A thief must go to the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me."
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod; Mn 8.315.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.

The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
But men who have committed sins, once they have been punished by kings,
go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
But he who takes a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who breaks a water-trough,
shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place.
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property shall be returned to its owner.
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments, death is the penalty when the amount exceeds one hundred.
But for a value exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should impose a fine eleven times the value.
For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially women,
as well as for the theft of the most precious gems, one deserves the death penalty.
Upon considering the time and the purpose, the king shall determine the punishment for the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicinal herbs.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for piercing them with a knife,
and likewise for the theft of cattle, one must immediately undergo the *ardhapādika* penance.
Of thread, cotton, fermenting agents, cow-dung, molasses, curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass; Mn 8.326.
For the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, as well as salts, and likewise for the theft of earthenware, earth, or ashes; Mn 8.327.
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of ghee,
of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
For other such intoxicating drinks, for cooked rice,
and for all kinds of prepared foods, the fine shall be double their value.
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*.
When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been cleaned,
the fine shall be one hundred panas for a first offense, and fifty panas if it has been committed repeatedly.
An act committed by force, provided it is accompanied by a claim of ownership, is considered *sāhasa* (violence);
whereas taking property secretly and then denying it constitutes *steya* (theft).
But the king shall punish first that man who steals these prepared articles, as well as whoever would steal the fire from the house.
With whatever limb a thief commits an offense against men,
that very limb the king shall take away as a deterrent.
Neither father, nor teacher, nor friend, nor mother, nor wife, nor son, nor domestic priest—
there is no one who, failing to abide by his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
For a Brahmin, it shall be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he is indeed one who knows both the faults and the merits of that [offense].
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, does not constitute theft.
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given,
even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching, is just like a thief.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be fined.
One who binds those who are not bound, releases those who are bound,
and seizes the slaves, horses, and chariots of others, shall incur the guilt of a thief.
By suppressing thieves according to this rule,
a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, eternal fame should not overlook a man of violent deeds even for a moment.
A man who commits an act of violence through harsh speech, theft, or even by means of physical punishment,
should be known as the worst among evildoers.
But that king who tolerates one engaged in violence quickly goes to ruin and incurs hatred.
Neither for the sake of a friend nor from the acquisition of vast wealth should a king release perpetrators of violence who bring fear to all living beings.
The twice-born may take up arms when their duty is obstructed,
or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the castes caused by the exigencies of time.
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in defense of women and Brahmins, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma.
One may indeed kill, without hesitation, an assailant who approaches, whether he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin.
In the killing of an *ātātāyin* (one who comes with intent to kill), no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer, whether it is done openly or secretly; for wrath recoils upon that wrath.
The king, having punished with terrifying punishments those men who have set out to violate another's wife, should banish them.
For from that arises the confusion of castes among people,
by which unrighteousness, destroying the very root, leads to universal ruin.
A man who engages in conversation with another's wife in secret,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out for a valid reason,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, in a forest,
or even at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery.
Attending upon her, playful dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments, and even sitting together on the same bed— all this is declared to be adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*).
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he permits her to touch him when she does so,
it is all considered *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct) provided there is mutual consent.
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected with the utmost care.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice,
and artisans may converse with women without being restrained.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
however, one who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own wives;
for they entice women and secretly employ them as spies.
However, he who engages in conversation with such women,
or with female slaves who eat only a single meal a day, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine.
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
however, a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in status, shall not suffer death.
One should not cause a maiden who is associating with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one who is serving an inferior man should be kept confined in the house.
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
one who has intercourse with a woman of equal caste shall pay a fee, if her father so desires.
But the man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
shall have two fingers instantly cut off and deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who defiles an unwilling one— namely, the cutting off of a finger—
but he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred paṇas to prevent a recurrence.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being dragged along by a donkey.
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, should transgress against her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with many people.
They should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon him there, and the evildoer shall be consumed by fire.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise, for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī*, the fine is exactly that much.

A Śūdra who cohabits with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she be protected or unprotected—is deprived of his limbs and all his property if she was unprotected, and of everything if she was protected. (Manu Smṛti 8.374)
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
he should fine the Vaiśya five hundred and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of them, having violated a guarded Brahmin woman,
shall be punished like Śūdras or shall be burned on a straw fire.
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred.
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa that ends with his life;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends with their lives.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and his body unharmed.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
If a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a protected Vaiśya woman,
both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman.
A Brāhmaṇa who approaches guarded women of the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya castes should be made to pay a fine of one thousand; for approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
If a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, the fine shall be five hundred;
however, the Kṣatriya should prefer either shaving his head with urine or paying that same fine.

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyajastri), he shall be fined one thousand.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with impunity, shares in the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power among his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world.
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—
provided that each is capable of the rite and free from fault— the punishment for both of them is one hundred [paṇas] each.
Neither a mother, nor a father, nor a wife, nor a son deserves to be abandoned;
he who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their status, shall be fined six hundred by the king.
When twice-born men in hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties,
a king who desires his own welfare should not pronounce a legal decision himself.
Having honored these men according to their merit along with the Brahmins,
and having first pacified them with gentle words, the king should establish them in their own duty.
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor when twenty worthy twice-born men are being fed at an auspicious occasion, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.
If a learned man does not feed another learned and virtuous man during auspicious rites,
he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold.
One who is blind, one who is mentally infirm, one who moves about on a board, and one who is seventy years old or older,
as well as one who serves those learned in the Vedas— none of these should be made to pay tax by anyone.
The king should always honor one learned in the Vedas, those afflicted by disease or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous.
On a smooth board made of śālmalī wood, a washerman shall wash clothes gently;
he shall not rub garments against one another, nor shall he let them dry together.
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread with an increase of one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve panas.
Those skilled at customs stations and expert in evaluating all types of merchandise shall determine the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.
If one exports out of greed those articles of the king that are well-known or prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property.
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
and one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
Having investigated the arrival, departure, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he shall regulate their purchase and sale.
Every five nights, or else at the end of every fortnight,
the king should personally perform the ritual offering of the guest-water (argha) for them.
All scales and measures must be well-marked;
every six months, one should have them re-examined.
A vehicle shall pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter paṇa; and an empty-handed man, half of that quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they possess.
On a long journey, one should know that a ferry may be available according to the place and the time on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such certainty on the ocean.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering ascetic,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll when crossing a river.
Whatever on a boat may be damaged through the negligence of the boatmen,
that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together from their own respective shares.
This decision regarding legal procedure for those traveling by boat has been declared:
in the case of water damage caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment; but in the case of an act of God, there is none at all.
One should cause a Vaiśya to practice trade, moneylending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and a Śūdra [should perform] service for the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa should support out of compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.
But a Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed and by virtue of his superior power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will,
shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, one should compel to perform service;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, and who can remove it from him? (Manu 8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given, one inherited from a father, and one enslaved by way of punishment— these seven are the sources of slavery.
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
A Brahmin may confidently take property from a Śūdra, for he possesses nothing of his own; indeed, his wealth is to be taken by his master.
The king should cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own respective duties with diligence; for if these two deviate from their own duties, they would throw this entire world into turmoil.
Day after day, he should inspect his undertakings and vehicles,
as well as income and expenditure, the mines, and the treasury itself.
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.
I shall now declare the eternal duties for a man and a woman who abide by the path of dharma, both in their union and in their separation.
Women must be kept under dependence by their own men day and night; and if they become attached to sensual pleasures, they must be restrained within their own control. (Manu 9.2)
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable, and a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
but when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.
Women must be protected especially from even the slightest of opportunities for misconduct;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring sorrow upon two families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all social classes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak.
For by diligently protecting his wife, a man protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (Manu Smṛti 9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife and become an embryo, is born here;
for that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard a woman with great effort.
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded by the employment of these following means.
He should employ her in the collection and expenditure of wealth,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
Those women who, though confined at home by trustworthy male guardians,
protect themselves by their own efforts, are truly well-protected.

Drinking intoxicants, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at improper times], and dwelling in the house of another—these six are the vices that corrupt women. (Manu 9.13)
They do not examine their appearance, nor is there any regard for their age;
whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection,
these women turn against their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
Having thus understood their nature as born from the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection.
Manu ordained that women should be deprived of beds, seats, ornaments, as well as desire, anger, dishonesty, ignobility, a malicious disposition, and misconduct.
"There is no ritual action for women with sacred mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma.
For women are without [Vedic] authority and devoid of mantras; it is settled that falsehood resides in women. (Manu 9.18)
And likewise, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas;
listen now to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics.
"Whatever my mother, wandering unfaithful, lusted for—that seed let my father take up"; this is the illustration of that [law]. (Manu 9.20)
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind for the sake of her husband,
this is declared to be the proper means of removing that transgression.
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule,
such qualities she acquires, just as a river does from the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerability through her union with Vasiṣṭha;
and Śāraṅgī attained the same status through Mandapāla.
These and other women of low birth in this world have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in their worldly life, which yields happiness both in this world and after death; now learn the duties concerning progeny.
For the sake of procreation, highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
there is no difference whatsoever between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) within households.
The procreation of offspring, the protection of those born, and the daily course of worldly life—women are the visible foundation for all this. (Manu Smṛti 9.27)
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent on her.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been proclaimed by the virtuous and by the great seers of old concerning a son.
They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict of scriptural authorities regarding the progenitor.
Some say he belongs to the one who produces him, while others know him to belong to the owner of the field.
The woman is traditionally regarded as the field, and the man is traditionally regarded as the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed.
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time,
that very kind of seed grows therein, manifested with its own inherent qualities.
For this earth is called the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth.
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers grow here in various forms according to their own nature.
Rice, śāli rice, mung beans, sesame seeds, māṣa beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcanes, sprout according to their respective seeds. (Manu 9.39)
"That one thing is sown and another is born" is not tenable;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth.
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a man should not sow seed in what belongs to another... (Manu 9.42).
Just as an arrow shot by one who pierces after another has already pierced a mark in the sky vanishes,
so indeed does seed sown in the possession of another quickly perish.
Those who know the past recognize this earth as the wife of Pṛthu;
they say that the field of Śālyavat was the clearing of Sthāṇuccheda.
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have declared; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (Manu 9.45)
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati.
A share of inheritance is distributed but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once;
and one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once among the virtuous.
Just as one who begets offspring on cows, mares, female camels, slave-girls, buffaloes, goats, or sheep does not share in the ownership of those offspring, so it is likewise with the wives of others.
Those who possess seed but do not own a field, and sow it in another's field, never obtain any fruit from the crop that has grown there. (Manu 9.49)
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another’s field benefit the owner of the field; the sower of the seed does not obtain the fruit.

But when no agreement regarding the fruit has been made between the owner of the field and the sower, the benefit clearly belongs to the owners of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed. (Manu 9.52)
But when seed is given for the purpose of sowing because of an agreement regarding the labor,
both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in the crop.
If seed carried by a flood of water sprouts in someone's field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. (Manu Smṛti 9.54)
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood.
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress.
The wife of an elder brother is the wife of a guru for the younger brother;
but the wife of a younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law for the elder.

An elder brother who approaches the wife of his younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of his elder brother— even if they have been authorized to do so— become outcasts, unless there be a time of distress.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring.
But a man appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent, may procreate one son during the night, but never a second under any circumstances.
Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [duty],
seeing that the purpose of the appointment (niyoga) for those two is not fully accomplished according to dharma.
When the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been accomplished according to the rule,
the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.
If those two, being appointed, should act according to their own will, disregarding the prescribed rule,
they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma.
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is "authorization" (niyoga) mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies.
For this practice, which is censured by learned twice-born men as being the law of beasts,
was declared even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
In former times, while enjoying the entire earth, that most excellent of royal sages,
his mind struck down by lust, brought about the intermixture of the social classes.
From that time forward, the virtuous censure any man who, out of delusion, engages a woman whose husband has died for the sake of offspring.
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall marry her according to this following rule.
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she who is dressed in white garments and observes pure vows—
