they should unite with one another once at each menstrual period until conception.
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again;
for by giving her once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being.
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rule, he may abandon a maiden who is blameworthy,
diseased, defiled, or one who was offered through deception.
But if one should bestow a girl who has defects without having disclosed them,
he shall annul that gift of the wicked-minded giver of the bride.
A man who has business to attend to may go abroad after providing for his wife's maintenance;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live adhering to her prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should subsist by means of blameless crafts.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be awaited for eight years;
for the sake of knowledge or fame, for six years; but for the sake of pleasure, for three years.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who hates him;
but after a year has passed, he may take her property and cease to live with her.
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.

There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, barren, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any exclusion from inheritance for her if she is hostile [to him].
A wife who drinks liquor, is of bad conduct, or is hostile;
or one who is diseased, injurious, or constantly wasteful of wealth—such a woman may indeed be superseded by another.
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately.
But a wife who is sickly, yet beneficial and endowed with virtuous character, may be superseded only after she has been informed; she must never be treated with contempt.
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should depart from the house in anger,
must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family.
If a woman, though forbidden, should nevertheless drink liquor even on festive occasions, or should go to a theatrical performance or a social assembly, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
If twice-born men marry women both of their own class and of other classes,
seniority, honor, and the right to the household shall belong to them according to the order of their castes.
A wife alone shall perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [the deceased husbands];
never may one who is not of the same caste do so in any way.
But he who, out of delusion, causes that [rite] to be performed by another woman of his own caste who is already established [in marriage],
is just like a "Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla" as previously described.
To one who is distinguished, handsome, excellent, and worthy,
he should give his daughter according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age.
A maiden may indeed remain in her father's house until death even if she has reached puberty;
however, he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may seek a husband of equal status.
If she should obtain a husband on her own initiative when she is not being given away,
she incurs no sin, nor does he whom she obtains.
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself the ornaments belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brothers; if she should take them, she would be a thief.
One who takes a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his authority as master.
A man thirty years of age should marry a pleasing girl of twelve years;
or one twenty-four years old may marry an eight-year-old, if he is in haste to fulfill his religious duty.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman.
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both husband and wife.
If the giver of the nuptial fee should die after the fee has been paid for a maiden,
she should be given to his brother-in-law, provided that the maiden consents.
Even a Śūdra should not take a bride-price when giving away his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price, he effects a concealed sale of his daughter.
But this is what neither others nor any other virtuous men have ever done: that having promised something to one person, it is then given to another. (Manu 9.99)
Indeed, we have never heard of such a thing even in former births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
Let there be mutual fidelity until death;
this, in brief, should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife.
Likewise, a man and a woman who have performed their rites should always strive so that,
even when separated from one another, they do not violate their mutual fidelity.
This duty of women and men, connected with sexual pleasure, has been declared to you, as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress; now learn the law concerning inheritance.
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive.
The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of the eldest son, a man becomes a father of a son and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, that son deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off a debt, and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as sons born of desire.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father.
The eldest son causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder is like a mother and like a father;
but he who does not behave as an elder should be honored merely like a kinsman.
Thus they may live together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma.
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, as well as the best item from among all the property;
half of that shall be the share of the middle son, and a fourth for the youngest.
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall receive the middle portion of the wealth.
The eldest son shall take the best of all kinds of property, as well as whatever is particularly excellent; he shall also receive one choice item from each group of ten.
There is no division into ten shares for those who have performed their own duties;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the elder, which increases his honor.
Thus, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should assign equal portions;
but if no preferential shares are set aside, this shall be the distribution of shares for them.
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the one born after him, a share and a half;
and the younger sons, each a single share—thus the law is established.
The brothers shall each separately give to their unmarried sisters a fourth part from their own respective shares; those who refuse to give shall become outcasts.
He should never divide goats, sheep, and one-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that goats and sheep may be divided unequally in favor of the eldest alone.
If a younger brother should beget a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law.
Subordination of the principal is not logically consistent with the law;
since the father is the principal in procreation, one should therefore honor him according to the law.

If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in a case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife, [the rule is as follows]. // Mn 9.122 //
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
thereafter, the other bulls, inferior to that, belong to those who are junior according to their mothers.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull as his special share and sixteen more [cows];
thereafter, the remaining sons shall divide the rest according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority based on the mother; seniority is said to be determined by birth [from the father].
It is recorded in the Subrahmaṇyā formulas that the invocation is made according to birth-order;
and even in the case of twins conceived in the womb, seniority is recorded as being determined by birth.
A sonless man may, by this rule, appoint a daughter as his "appointed daughter" (putrikā), with the agreement: "Whatever offspring shall be born of her shall be the performer of my funeral rites."
In former times, Dakṣa himself, the lord of creatures, created these daughters according to this rule for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
With a joyful heart, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them with due respect.
As one's self is, so is one's son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's own self, how could another take the wealth? (Manu Smṛti 9.130)
Whatever may be the mother's separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the share of the unmarried daughter;
and the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire estate of one who dies without a son.
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
In this world, there is no difference between a son’s son and a daughter’s son according to the law,
for both of them were produced from the bodies of their respective parents.
But if, after a daughter has been appointed [as an heir], a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without having borne a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.

Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if she bears a son who resembles [the father], through that son the maternal grandfather becomes the recipient of the *pinda* offerings and shall inherit the wealth. (Manu 9.136)
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
In this world, no distinction is found between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers him to the next world, just like a son’s son.
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to her father’s father.
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall never inherit the family name or the estate of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and the estate, and the *svadhā* offering ceases for one who gives it to the wrong lineage.

Both the son born of a woman not authorized [to bear children] and the son obtained from a brother-in-law by a woman who already has a son do not deserve a share; they are born of an adulterer and born of lust.
Even if born of a woman duly appointed,
a son produced contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to his father's inheritance, for he was procreated by one who has fallen from his status.
A son born to a woman appointed for that purpose is considered equal to a legitimate son of the body;
according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring.
He who takes charge of the wealth and the widow of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him.
If a woman, being authorized by another, obtains a son from her brother-in-law or another [kinsman],
they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and born in vain.
This rule for partition among those born of a single womb from one man should be understood;
now learn [the rule] regarding those born of many women of different castes from one man. Mn 9.148.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order [of castes],
this rule for the division [of the estate] is prescribed when sons have been born to them.
A ploughman, a bull, a vehicle, ornaments, and a house—
these should be given as the special share (oddhārika) to the Brāhmaṇa, along with one principal portion from the remainder.
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya wife two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya wife one and a half shares; and the son of a Śūdra wife shall take one share.
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the law should perform a righteous partition according to this rule.
A son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
Even if he should have a virtuous son or even no son at all,
one must not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra wife.
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya is not an heir to the estate;
whatever his father may give him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste for the twice-born may all divide the estate equally after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other;
the sons born of her shall have equal shares, even if there should be a hundred sons.
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has mentioned for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the son made, the son secretly born, and the son cast off— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a defective boat obtains a corresponding result,
so too does one who attempts to cross the darkness [of rebirth] with bad sons obtain a corresponding result.
If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are co-heirs,
each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other.
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of compassion toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood.
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja),
or even a fifth share.
The son begotten on one's own wife (aurasa) and the son born of the wife of another (kṣetraja) are both entitled to a share of the father's inheritance;
however, ten other types of sons, in their respective order, are entitled only to a share of the family name and the inheritance.
One should know that son whom he himself begets upon his own wedded wife to be the legitimate (aurasa) son of the first order.
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased, to a woman duly appointed according to the sacred law, is known as a *kṣetraja* (son of the wife).
If, in times of distress, the mother or the father should give a son who is similar [to themselves] and with affection, accompanied by water, he is to be known as a "given" (dattrima) son.
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the *kṛtrima* (artificial) son.
But he who is born in a house and whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he shall belong to him by whom he was begotten on the wife.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha*.
But the son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father’s house, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born from the maiden, not from the husband.
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown,
the child belongs to the husband and is called "sahoḍha" (one born with the bride).
If one should purchase from his mother or father a son for the sake of offspring,
that son is his "bought" (krītaka) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [to him].
She who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces offspring again of her own will after marrying once more, is called *paunarbhava*.
If she is still a virgin, even if she has returned after having left,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her husband from a second marriage.
He who, being deprived of his parents or abandoned by them without cause,
offers himself to someone, is known as a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) son.
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may procreate through lust upon a Śūdra woman is a corpse even while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.
Whether born of a Śūdra’s slave-woman or the slave-woman of a slave, the son who is thus born shall, with permission, take a share; such is the established law.
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as described above, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as born from the seed of others belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else.
Manu has declared that among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son.
If among all the wives who have but one husband, even one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
In the absence of a superior [claimant], one who is inferior is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate.
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are the heirs to the estate of the father;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, and so too shall the brothers.
Water must be offered to three; the funeral ball (piṇḍa) proceeds for three;
the fourth is the giver of these; a fifth is not possible.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda;
after him, it shall go to a sakulya, or else to the teacher or the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs of the estate; thus the Dharma is not violated.

"The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; such is the settled rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take their property when there is a total absence [of heirs]."
For one who has died childless, one should procure a son from a member of the same lineage;
whatever wealth there may be, that one should bestow upon him.
But if two [sons] should dispute over the property of their mother, both born from her,
each shall take that which belonged to his own father, and not the other.
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally.
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection.

That which is given before the nuptial fire, that which is received from the father's family at the wedding, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
The property given as a post-nuptial gift (anvādheya), as well as that which was given by the husband out of affection,
shall belong to the children of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.

Whatever property was acquired during marriages according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites, it is ordained that, upon the death of the wife without issue, it belongs to the husband alone.
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that upon her death childless, it shall belong to her mother and father.
Whatever wealth may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring.
Women shall not make a disposal from the family property held in common by many,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their own husband.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do so fall from their caste.
Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.
However, it is right for a wise man to give to all of them food and clothing to the best of his ability; for he who does not give becomes an outcast.
If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others,
their offspring, having produced a lineage, shall be entitled to the inheritance.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died,
the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning.
But if all those who were unlearned should acquire wealth through their own exertion,
it is the settled rule that there should be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property.
But whatever constitutes his wealth acquired through learning—that alone shall be his property;
as shall that received through friendship, that received at marriage, and that received with the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka).
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth, shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence. (Manu 9.207)
That which has been acquired by one's own effort through labor, without depleting the paternal estate—
that which was obtained by one's own exertion— one is not obliged to give away against one's will.
But if a father recovers ancestral property that had been lost,
he need not share it with his sons against his will, as it was acquired by himself.
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that instance.
If the eldest or the youngest [son] should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them should die, his share is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having assembled together, shall divide it equally;
so too shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall forfeit his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings.

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should an elder brother make a separate provision for himself without having given anything to the younger brothers.
If there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who have not divided their inheritance,
the father must under no circumstances allot unequal shares among their sons.
But one who is born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide it with them.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother also has passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
When all debts and assets have been divided according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be made equal.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession, and pasture land— they declare these to be indivisible.
This division of property for you and the rule for the performance of rites for sons born of the wife and the others has been declared in due order; now learn the law concerning gambling.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the end of kings who rule the earth.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
whereas that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya). (Mn 9.223)
The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
He should quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, cruel men, those who adhere to heretical sects, those who follow improper occupations, and liquor-sellers.
These, existing as secret thieves within the kingdom,
constantly oppress the virtuous subjects through their illicit actions.
In a former age, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not practice gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whether it be done in secret or openly, whatever man should practice such [forbidden acts],
there shall be a variety of punishments for him according to the king's discretion.
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who is unable to pay a fine shall discharge his debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it back gradually.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king should administer punishment using whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like.
But those who, having been appointed to official duties,
ruin the affairs of litigants while being consumed by the fever of greed, the king shall deprive them of their property.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies.
Whatever has been adjudicated and instructed in any matter whatsoever, one should know that to be settled according to dharma; one must not reverse it again.
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly,
the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
And for these four who do not perform penance,
he shall prescribe a lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.

For violating the teacher's bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
Indeed, being unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice for, unfit to teach, and unfit to marry,
they shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties.
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives;
they shall be without compassion and without salutation—this is the instruction of Manu.
But those of all castes who perform the prescribed penance as declared shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa alone, the middle amercement shall be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his property and belongings.
But those others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; if, however, they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt.
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Where the king avoids deriving wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time with long lives.
And the crops of the people ripen according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and nothing deformed is born.
But a king should slay with various terrifying methods of execution that person of low caste who, out of lust, oppresses Brahmins.
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; but merit accrues to him who exercises restraint.
Thus has been declared in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties engaged in mutual dispute regarding the eighteen titles of law.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with the Dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet gained and protect those already acquired.
But having settled in a suitable location and constructed a fortress according to the treatises,
he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to heaven.
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves—
his kingdom becomes agitated and he falls away from heaven.
But that kingdom which is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered.
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret. Mn 9.256.
Those who live by various wares are "open cheats," while those such as thieves and forest-dwellers are "concealed cheats."
Those who take bribes, those who practice fraud, cheats, gamblers, those who live by predicting auspicious events, fortune-tellers, and those who examine bodily marks for luck; Mn 9.258.
Likewise, high officials who act improperly, physicians, those skilled in the practice of crafts, and clever courtesans; Mn 9.259.
One should recognize such manifest thorns of the world as these, as well as others who move in disguise—ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble. (Manu 9.260)
Having discovered them through well-conducted secret agents who perform those specific tasks and through spies in various disguises, he should incite them and bring them under his control.

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king should duly administer punishment based on the gravity of the offense and the strength of the offender.
For indeed, without punishment,
it is impossible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who harbor evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles. Mn 9.264.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans, as well as empty houses, groves, and pleasure-grounds; Mn 9.265.
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military units, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
He should discover them through their companions who follow them and are familiar with their various activities,
and he should eliminate them by means of clever former thieves.
They should bring about their meeting by means of instructions regarding food and drink, by visiting Brahmins,
and by discussions of heroic deeds.
Those who do not approach him there, and those who are instigators from the root,
the king shall forcibly slay, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen property;
however, he may execute one caught with the stolen goods along with the implements used for the theft, without hesitation.
Moreover, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves or give them shelter for their goods— all of those as well he shall cause to be executed.
He should swiftly punish those appointed to protect the realms and the feudal lords who have been incited, as well as those who remain neutral during attacks, just like thieves.
And even one who lives by the Dharma but has fallen away from the covenant of the Dharma— he too,
having strayed from his own duty, should be consumed by punishment alone.

Those who do not run to the aid of others to the best of their ability when a village is being plundered, when a well is being destroyed, or when a robbery is seen on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings.
He shall cause those who embezzle the king’s treasury, those who stand in opposition to him,
and those who instigate his enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment.
But those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking through a wall—
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake.
In the first instance of breaking a seal, one should have the fingers of the thief cut off;
in the second, his hand and foot; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
The king should punish like a thief those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter to robbers, as well as those who act as their accomplices.
One who destroys a tank should be killed, or else executed by drowning in water;
or, if he should repair it, he should be made to pay the highest fine.
One should indeed put to death, without hesitation, those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots.
But he who diverts the water of a pre-existing tank,
or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
He who, except in an emergency, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity.
Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child deserve only a verbal reprimand, and that [offense] must be purified; such is the settled rule.
For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement in the case of non-human beings, but the middle amercement in the case of human beings.
One who breaks the arches, flagstaffs,
or images shall repair all of that damage and pay five hundred panas as a fine.
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods,
as well as for their breaking or the fraudulent boring of gems, the punishment is the first amercement.
For a man who treats equals unequally, whether in conduct or even in price,
shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement.
And the king should establish all places of confinement along the road,
where those who have committed evil deeds may be seen suffering and disfigured.
One should immediately banish anyone who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat, or destroys a gate.
In all cases of malevolent sorcery, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for root-magic and various types of witchcraft, until such acts have been brought to an end.
One who sells seeds, one who steals seeds,
and likewise one who violates the boundaries [of fields], shall suffer the punishment of mutilation or death.
But a king shall have a goldsmith who is the most wicked of all thorns,
if he persists in unlawful conduct, cut into pieces with razors.
In cases of the theft of Sītā-grain, weapons, or medicine,
the king, having considered the time and the purpose, shall determine the punishment.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital city, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Among these seven constituent elements of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one is more serious and its calamity greater than the next.
In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels anything else because of the specific excellence of their mutual qualities.
In various specific tasks, however, one particular limb excels;
that by which a specific purpose is accomplished is said to be the most excellent for that task.
Through his movements, through the application of energy, and indeed through the performance of his duties,
the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain both his own strength and the strength of his enemy.
Having reflected upon the gravity or lightness of all oppressions as well as calamities, he should then undertake his task.
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages—all these are the conduct of kings; for the king is said to be the age itself.
When asleep, he is the Kali age; when awake, he is the Dvāpara age;
when intent upon actions, he is the Tretā age; but when wandering about, he is the Kṛta age.
A king should conduct himself with the splendor and the conduct of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and Pṛthivī. (Manu 9.303)
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should he who observes the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the objects of desire.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should he take taxes from his kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun.
Just as the wind moves about having entered all living beings, so should one enter [among them] by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-like" vow.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should he restrain evil-doers; for this is the vow of Varuṇa.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do his subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow.
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a slayer of wicked vassals— that is known as the Agneya vow.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings.
Employing these and other means, the king, ever vigilant, should suppress thieves within his own kingdom and even in those of others.
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke the Brāhmaṇas;
for they, when angered, could instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts.
Who would not perish by provoking those by whom fire was made to consume everything, the great ocean was rendered undrinkable, and the waning moon was made to wax? (Mn 9.314)
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked to anger, might create other worlds and world-protectors, or turn gods into non-gods? (Manu 9.315)
Those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, and for whom Brahman itself is their wealth—who, desiring to live, would harm them? (Manu 9.316)
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is a great deity, just as fire is a great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when oblations are offered to it in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable activities,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme deity.
When the Kṣatriya power has become excessively overbearing toward Brāhmaṇas in every respect, the Brāhmaṇical power alone shall be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
Neither the Kṣatriya power without the Brahmanic power prospers, nor does the Brahmanic power without the Kṣatriya power increase;
but when the Brahmanic and Kṣatriya powers are united, they flourish both in this world and in the next.
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle.
Acting thus and always disciplined in the duties of a king, the monarch should employ all his servants in what is beneficial for the world.
This entire eternal rule of action has been declared for the king;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order.
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the sacraments and taken a wife,
should be constantly engaged in agriculture and trade, as well as in the protection of cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya should have no desire to think, "I will not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya is willing, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
One should know the relative value and worth of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven fabrics, perfumes, and liquids.
He should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the soil;
he should understand the application of measures and all the applications of weights.
He should understand the value and worthlessness of merchandise, the merits and defects of regions,
the profit and loss on commodities, and the breeding of livestock.
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their purchase and sale.
He should exert the greatest effort to increase his wealth through righteous means,
and he should diligently provide food for all living beings.
For a Śūdra, however, the highest dharma leading to supreme beatitude is solely the service of illustrious householders who are Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
Pure, devoted to excellent service, gentle in speech, free from egoism,
and always taking refuge in Brahmins and the like, one attains a superior birth.
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them even in times of distress.
The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound [the Veda], and not the other two.
The Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all according to the rule;
he should proclaim them to the others and should himself likewise abide by them.
Due to his distinction, the excellence of his origin, his observance of restrictive rules,
and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth, however, is once-born, the Śūdra; there is no fifth.
Among wives of equal caste from all social orders who have not lost their virginity,
those born in the direct order of castes (ānulomyena) should be known as belonging to that very same caste.
Sons begotten by the twice-born on women born immediately after them in the social order are said to be similar [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower.
From a Brāhmaṇa on a Vaiśya maiden is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra maiden is born a Niṣāda, who is also called a Pāraśava. (Manu 10.8)
From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Śūdra is born a being named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.
These six are declared to be base-born (apasada): those born from a Brāhmaṇa in the [lower] three castes, those from a Kṣatriya in two castes, and those from a Vaiśya in one caste.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa maiden is born a Sūta by birth;
from a Vaiśya [on such maidens] are born a Māgadha and a Vaideha, who are the sons of a king and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.
From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men— these being the offspring of the mixture of castes.
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and the Ugra are recorded as resulting from the natural order when there is an interval of one caste,
so too are the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka born from the inverse order.

Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife of the same caste] in order are designated by the name "anantara" (immediate) because of the defect of their mothers.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one called Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra; but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra through women of the higher castes in the reverse order.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, only the Sūta is born.
These others are also three base-born (apasada) sons who are born in the inverse order.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pukkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka.
One born from a Kṣattṛ by an Ugrā woman is known as a Śvapāka;
but one produced by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhā woman is called a Veṇa.
Those whom the twice-born beget upon wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of vows,
one should designate as *vrātyas*, fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*.
From a Vrātya Brāhmaṇa are born the evil-natured Bhūrjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.
From the Rājanya Vratya are born the Jhalla, the Malla, the Nicchivi,
the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Through adultery, through the marrying of those who should not be married,
and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises.
But those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural unions,
and those who are mutually intermingled— I shall describe them in their entirety.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Āyogava, and the Kṣattṛ caste.
These six beget similar castes upon women of their own kind;
they are born from mothers of the same caste as themselves, and also from women of higher castes.
Just as for the three castes, a son is born from two [wives] of the same caste,
so too among the outcastes (bāhya), by immediate succession, a son is born from his own kind.
And they also procreate upon the wives of others many outsiders who are even more corrupted than themselves and are held in contempt.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste child upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, so does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste upon women of the four castes.
Acting in opposition to their own kind, those who are outsiders beget even more outsiders; being low, they give birth to fifteen further degraded castes.
From a Dasyu and an Āyogava woman is born a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply cosmetics and attend to personal adornment, yet is not a slave but lives like one, subsisting by means of snares.
The Vaideha begets a Maitreyaka from a Mādhūka woman;
he constantly praises men and strikes a bell at the break of dawn.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by working with boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.
These three distinct low-born castes are born from Āyogava women who wear the clothes of the dead and eat despised food.
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born as a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehika are born the Āndhra and Meda, who have their dwellings outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī woman is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī woman.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pukkasa woman, is born a sinful Sopāka, whose livelihood consists of the root of calamity and who is always censured by the virtuous.
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman gives birth to a son called an Antyāvasāyin,
who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the pale.
These castes resulting from intermixture, as indicated by their fathers and mothers,
are to be known— whether they are concealed or manifest— by their respective occupations.

The six sons born of women of their own caste or of those immediately below them possess the status of the twice-born; however, all those born of women further removed are recorded as being of the same nature as Śūdras, born of a violation of the natural order.
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.
But these Kṣatriya castes have gradually attained the state of Śūdras in this world through the neglect of their duties and the absence of Brāhmaṇas.
The Pauṇḍrakas, the Auḍras, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas,
the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, the Daradas, and the Khaśas.

Those castes in the world who are outside of those born from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet— whether they speak the language of barbarians or the language of the Āryas— are all traditionally known as Dasyus.
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions,
should subsist by means of the despised occupations of the twice-born themselves.
For Sūtas, the management of horses and chariots; for Ambaṣṭhas, the practice of medicine;
for Vaidehakas, attendance on women; and for Māgadhas, the way of trade.
The killing of fish is the duty of Niṣādas; that of Āyogavas is carpentry;
and for Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus, it is the slaughter of wild animals.
But for the Kṣattragus, Pukkasas, and Bilaukovas, their livelihood consists of killing and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, working with hides; and for the Veṇas, playing drums.
These learned men shall dwell at sacred shrines, by trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves, subsisting by their own prescribed duties.
The dwellings of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, however, shall be outside the village;
they must be provided with broken vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their clothing shall be the garments of the dead, their food from broken vessels,
their ornament iron, and they must always maintain the life of a wandering mendicant.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them;
their mutual dealings and marriages should be only with their own equals.
Their food, which must be given by others, should be served in separate vessels;
they shall not wander at night through villages or towns.
They may go about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the disposal of a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the settled rule.
And they shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures and by the king's command;
they shall also take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of the executed.
One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of caste, unknown, born of a defiled womb, and who, though appearing noble in form, is actually ignoble.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty,
and an inactive nature reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb.
He inherits the character of his father, or of his mother, or of both;
for one of base birth cannot, under any circumstances, suppress his own innate nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there is a confusion of birth,
that man will surely adopt the conduct of that [lower caste], whether to a small or great extent.
But that kingdom where these corrupters of the castes are born through promiscuity perishes very quickly along with its inhabitants.
The unconditioned sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or a cow,
and for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those of foreign origin.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of the duty for the four castes.
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with a superior partner,
he attains the caste of his superior until the seventh generation.
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise falls to the status of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is also the case for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father upon a non-Aryan mother, and one born from a non-Aryan father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother? (Mn 10.66)

One born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan by his qualities; but one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is certainly a non-Aryan—this is the settled rule. (Manu 10.67)
The law is established that both of these are ineligible for sacramental rites:
the former because of the deficiency of his birth, and the latter because he is born in the inverse order.
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition,
so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement.
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established rule is as follows.
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren wasteland.
Since sages born of animal species became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is praised.
Having carefully considered one who is ignoble yet performs noble deeds, and one who is noble yet performs ignoble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Those Brahmins who abide in the source of the Veda and remain steadfast in their own duties should properly subsist by performing the six occupations in their proper order.
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices,
giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.
In the same way, these [prohibitions] shall cease with respect to a Vaiśya;
such is the settled rule, for Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them.
The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya.
But the duty for all is giving gifts, study, and sacrifice.
The study of the Vedas is the distinguished duty among one's own tasks for a Brāhmaṇa, protection for a Kṣatriya, and the occupation of trade and agriculture for a Vaiśya. (Manu 10.80)
But if a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own aforementioned duty,
he may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best alternative for him.
But if he should find it impossible to live by either of these, how should he proceed? He may subsist by adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, namely, agriculture and cattle-rearing.
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and is dependent on others.
People consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.
But for one who, due to a deficiency of livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma,
this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth, provided that the choice pieces have been extracted.
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, domestic animals, and human beings.
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as linen, silk, and woolen fabrics—
even if they should be undyed— as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass.
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals.
Having personally undertaken agriculture and produced [the crop], a farmer may sell sesamum seeds that are not yet fully ripened for the sake of dharma, provided they are of the *śūdra* variety.
If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than giving them as food or as an ointment,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors.
One falls immediately from one's status by selling meat, lac, or salt;
by selling milk, a Brahmin becomes a Śūdra within three days.
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for other flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal.
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all of this,
yet he must never at any time take pride in a livelihood superior to his own.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed,
the king, having deprived him of his wealth, shall banish him immediately.
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another;
for by living according to the duty of another, one immediately falls from one's caste.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts and, when capable, he desists from such conduct.
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born and has fallen into distress regarding his children and wife may live by the work of artisans.
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served are the duties of artisans.
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path and is suffering from the distress of lacking a means of subsistence, should practice this rule.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a purifier should become defiled—this is not logically tenable according to the Dharma.
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts— even if they are censurable— for they are like fire and water.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening crisis, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not tainted by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
Desiring to eat dog-meat when afflicted by hunger, Vāmadeva— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— was not defiled, for he did so for the sake of preserving his life.
But the great ascetic Bharadvāja, afflicted by hunger in the lonely forest along with his sons,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise from teaching,
for a Brahmin, the acceptance of gifts is the lowest [of these] and is censured after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those who have been consecrated;
however, the acceptance of gifts may even be performed from a Śūdra of the lowest birth.
Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed by renunciation and by austerity alone.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from various sources;
gathering ears of grain (śila) is better than receiving gifts, and picking up individual grains (uñcha) is praised even more than that.
If they are distressed, desiring base metals or wealth, Snātaka Brahmins may petition the lord of the earth; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.
From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, cattle, goats, sheep, gold, grain, and food—each preceding item is less blameworthy than the one following it.
There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, the performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Learning, a craft, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture,
contentment, begging, and usury are the ten means of livelihood.
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give a small amount to a sinful person.
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he may collect the lawful tribute.
The toll on grain for the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide labor, artisans, and craftsmen likewise [pay this].
But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, may serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek to live.
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both worlds, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his duty.
Service to the Brahmins alone is declared to be the distinguished duty of the Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him.
He should provide for their maintenance from his own family resources as is appropriate,
having regard for their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they support.
One should give him leftover food, worn-out clothes,
the dregs of grain, and old household utensils.
There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve any sacramental rite;
he has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against him from dharma.
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous,
do not incur sin by doing so— provided they avoid the recitation of mantras— and they even receive praise.
For in whatever measure a blameless person, free from envy, adheres to virtuous conduct,
in that same measure he attains both this world and the next.
For even a Śūdra who is capable should not engage in the accumulation of wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves. (Mn 10.129)
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by performing them correctly, they attain the supreme goal.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter I shall declare the auspicious rule for penance.

One who belongs to a lineage of sacrificers, one who is about to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking wealth for the sake of a teacher, for the sake of his father or mother, one desiring to study the Vedas, and one who is afflicted by illness. (Manu 11.1)
One should indeed know those Snātakas who are Brāhmaṇas seeking alms for the sake of dharma;
gifts should be given to these destitute ones according to the excellence of their learning.
For food accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial altar (vedī).
But the king should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice, according to their merit.
He who, having already taken a wife, obtains another by begging for her, gains only the pleasure of it as his reward; the offspring belongs, however, to the giver of the wealth.
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins according to one's ability—upon those learned in the Vedas and living in seclusion; thus, after death, one enjoys heaven.
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, that twice-born man who drinks Soma when the substance is very small,
even if he has previously drunk Soma, does not obtain its fruit.
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery—this is a mere semblance of dharma; it is like the taste of honey followed by the taste of poison.
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death.
If the sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the absence of even a single limb—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, while a righteous king is in power— then [the following applies].
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.
He may take three or two items at will from the house of a Śūdra,
for a Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices.
If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—
one may take from the households of even these two without hesitation.
If a person does not give what has been taken from one who is impermanent, it should be taken back from him;
thus his fame spreads and his merit increases.
Likewise, when he has fasted for six meals and is at the point of the seventh meal,
he may take food from one of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found,
that [stolen property] must be reported to the one who asks, provided he does indeed ask.
A Kṣatriya must never, under any circumstances, seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he may take the property of a Dasyu or one who neglects his religious duties if he has no other means of subsistence.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and carries both of them across.
The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods;
however, the property of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of the asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth must not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger.
Having ascertained his dependents and his own family members, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth shall provide them with a righteous means of livelihood.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from one thus protected, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit of dharma.
A Brahmin should never beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who has begged thus is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the purpose of a sacrifice, does not give it all away,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of a Brāhmaṇa—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures.

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the purpose of expiating any failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.
If a twice-born man performs a religious rite according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress,
it has been determined that he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter.
And by all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great seers,
when they were afraid of death in times of distress, a substitute for the prescribed rule was established.
The lord of the primary rule who conducts himself according to a secondary rule—
no fruit pertaining to the next world exists for that person of evil intellect.
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king regarding those human disciples who have done him harm; he should deal with them by his own power alone.
Between one's own prowess and the prowess of a king, one's own prowess is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own prowess alone.
Without hesitation, he may employ the hymns of the Atharva-Angirases;
for the weapon of a Brahmin is indeed speech, and with that, the twice-born man shall slay his enemies.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through silent recitation and burnt offerings.
One who ordains, instructs, and speaks with friendliness is called a Brāhmaṇa;
one should not speak what is unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool;
neither one who is afflicted by illness, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, should be the officiating priest for the Agnihotra.
For these fall into hell, as does he for whom they perform the sacrifice while offering oblations;
therefore, the officiating priest (hotṛ) should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.
If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, fails to give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya),
he remains one who has not established the fires.
One who is faithful and has conquered his senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, he should by no means perform sacrifices in this world with meager sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
If a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should, out of desire, abandon those fires, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice,
are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on Brahman.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of a *vṛṣala*, the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and is addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to penance.
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
some, however, declare it is required even for one committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scripture.
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of penances.
Having incurred the state of requiring expiation, whether by fate or by his own prior actions,
a twice-born man shall not associate with the virtuous as long as the expiation has not been performed.
In this world, some wicked men, as well as others due to their past deeds,
undergo a transformation of their physical form because of their misconduct.
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a slayer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the Guru’s bed, a skin disease.
A slanderer [attains] a putrid nose, a backbiter a foul-smelling mouth;
a stealer of grain suffers from physical deformity, while one who adulterates [grain] suffers from redundancy of limbs.
One who steals food suffers from chronic disease; one who steals speech becomes mute;
one who steals clothing suffers from leucoderma; and one who steals a horse becomes lame. (Manu 11.51)
Thus, by reason of specific actions, they are born despised by the virtuous;
likewise as dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, and deformed in appearance.
Therefore, one must always perform penance for the sake of purification;
for those whose sins are not expiated are born with censurable physical marks.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife, and association with those who commit these acts—these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka). Mn 11.54 [53M]
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, malicious talebearing directed toward the king,
and the persistent practice of deception toward a teacher are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Abandoning a Brahmin, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend,
eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.
They consider the emission of semen into women who are one's own uterine sisters, virgins, or women of the lowest castes,
as well as into the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the Guru's bed.

Killing a cow; officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice or sacrificing for such a person; adultery; selling oneself; abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, or son; and neglecting the private Vedic recitation or the sacred fires. (Manu 11.59)
The elder brother remaining unmarried while the younger is married is *parivitti*, and the younger brother marrying before the elder is *parivettṛ*;
[the sin of] giving away a daughter in marriage to either of them, or officiating as a priest for either of them; Mn 11.60.
Violating a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child; Mn 11.61.
The state of being a Vrātya, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages, receiving instruction from a servant, and the sale of goods that should not be sold; Mn 11.62.

Exercising authority over all forms [of work], operating great machines, dealing in harmful medicinal herbs, living off women, performing malevolent incantations (*abhicāra*), and performing root-rites (*mūlakarman*).
Felling green trees for the sake of fuel, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating censured food; Mn 11.64.
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts, studying under a wicked teacher, and the practice of the arts for mere livelihood; Mn 11.65.
The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; consorting with women who drink liquor;
the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these are minor offenses (upapātaka).
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are declared to be acts that cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats,
sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
Accepting wealth from those who are censured, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras, and speaking untruths— these are to be known as acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa).
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
Now, learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins are respectively expiated. Mn 11.71 [70M]
A killer of a Brahmin, having made a hut, shall dwell in the forest for twelve years for the sake of self-purification,
subsisting on alms and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
Or he may become a target for those who bear weapons, according to his own wish;
or he may throw himself headlong three times into a blazing fire.
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or, for the expiation of the murder of a Brahmin, he may travel one hundred yojanas to Japan or any other [holy place], eating sparingly and with his senses restrained.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas—
be it wealth sufficient for a livelihood or a house together with its furnishings.
Or, subsisting on sacrificial food, he should follow the Sarasvatī upstream;
or, with his diet restricted, he should recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage,
or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should immediately sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Or he who has resisted [a Brahmin] three times, or having seized all his property,
or having caused the loss of his life for that purpose, is released from [the sin].
Thus, one who is constant in firm vows, a celibate student, and composed in mind,
removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin at the completion of twelve years.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods on earth (Brahmins) in an assembly of kings,
he is liberated from it after bathing at the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Kṣatriya its summit;
therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified.
