By his very birth, he is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā alone is the cause in this matter.
Those three who know the Vedas shall declare for them a complete expiation for their sin;
that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying.
Therefore, by adhering to one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin,
through self-control, removes the sin committed by killing a Brahmin.
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], and likewise a woman who is an Ātreyī.
Having given false testimony, having obstructed a teacher, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; Mn 11.88.
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for killing a Brāhmaṇa intentionally, no atonement is prescribed.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he shall drink liquor that is red-hot like fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he should drink cow's urine as hot as fire, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or even the liquid of cow dung until death.
Or, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, he shall eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks, and carrying a skull-topped staff.
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā.
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are to be known as the three kinds of surā;
just as one is, so are all of them—they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation of the gods must not consume them.
A Brahmin, deluded by intoxication, might fall into impurity, or recite the Veda, or perform some other improper act. (Manu 11.96)
He whose Brahmanical nature, residing in his body, is once drenched by liquor—
his status as a Brahmin departs and he becomes a Śūdra.
This manifold expiation for drinking liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should declare his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me."
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove by austerity the impurity born of stealing gold,
shall wear rags and perform in the forest the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he should expiate the sin of approaching the teacher’s wife by means of these very same vows.
Having spoken with the wife of his guru, he should lie upon a heated iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing iron image of a woman; by death, he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his own penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms,
he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until he falls down.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard and dwelling in a lonely forest,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food or barley gruel, in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru's bed.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakinaḥ) may do so by means of these various kinds of vows.
A cow-killer who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his ablutions using cow urine.
During the day he should follow those cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust they raise;
having served them and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While [the others] stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should follow;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit, self-restrained and free from envy.
One should rescue by every possible means a woman who is ill or accused, or one threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen or is stuck in a mire.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
One should not report a cow eating in one's own house, or in the house of another, nor in a field or a threshing floor, nor a calf drinking milk. (Manu 11.114)
But he who, following this rule, attends upon a cow,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.
Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) should perform this very same vow for the sake of purification,
with the exception of the avakīrṇin rite, or else they may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
But one who has spilled his semen shall, at night, sacrifice a one-eyed donkey at a crossroads according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*, offering it to Nirṛti.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rule, and finally having come together with the [appropriate] verse,
he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni.
Those who know the Dharma and expound the Veda declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The fourfold Brahmanic splendor of one who has broken his vow approaches the Maruts, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka.
When this sin has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go about for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day,
and performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he becomes purified in one year.
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness to receive alms, the purification is the lunar penance (*aindava*) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who abides by his duties; and it should be known that for a Śūdra, it is a sixteenth part.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having observed his vow well, shall give a thousand cows and one bull.
Or, with his hair matted and self-restrained, he should perform for three years the penance prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin,
dwelling far from a village and making his home at the foot of a tree.
The best of the twice-born should perform this very penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his duties,
and he should also give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or he shall give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one shall perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Or he should drink milk for three nights, or walk a distance of one yojana,
or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn dedicated to the waters (Ab-daivata).
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
For killing a boar, one must give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a curlew, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, a peacock,
a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; having killed an elephant, five dark-colored bulls;
having killed a goat or a sheep, an ox; and having killed a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; and having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
Having killed women of unstable character belonging to any of the four castes, one should give separately for purification the hides of a Jina, a bow, and a bull.
If a twice-born man is unable to purify himself from the killing of snakes and other such creatures through the giving of gifts,
he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate beings,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
But for killing a vertebrate animal, one should give something to a Brahmin;
however, for injuring boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for cutting shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the means of purification.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the rules] regarding the eating of forbidden food.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone; but for intentional drinking, the penance is beyond prescription—it ends only with life—such is the settled rule.
Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for *surā* liquor or likewise in a vessel for intoxicating drinks,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rule,
or having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are discontinued for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Even after drinking fermented acids or astringent decoctions, though they are pure, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that substance has not passed downward.
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth,
or meat from a slaughterhouse that was not known [to have been killed for one's sake], one should observe this very same penance.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, cocks, humans, crows, and donkeys,
the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher's house should eat food given on the monthly ancestral offering (māsika),
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.
But a student of sacred knowledge who should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever,
having performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance, shall complete the remainder of his vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a rat, or those of a dog or a mongoose,
or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.
One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit for consumption;
however, if it was eaten through ignorance, it should be vomited up or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites.
Thus has been declared the various rule for the vows regarding the eating of forbidden food;
now hear the rule for those vows that remove the guilt of theft.
Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
But for the abduction of human women, as well as fields,
houses, wells, tanks, and water, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification.
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house,
one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that property.
For stealing food that is chewed or eaten, as well as vehicles, beds, seats,
flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver,
iron, brass, or stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed animals, single-hoofed animals, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk alone for three days.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these same vows.
Having discharged semen into women of his own kin, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, he shall perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed.
Having approached a daughter of his father’s sister, a daughter of his own sister,
or a daughter of his mother’s brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives;
they are not to be approached as kin, for by marrying them he falls low.
Having discharged semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper womb, or even into water, one shall perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance.
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman,
a twice-born man shall perform a bath along with his clothes in a bullock-cart, in water, or during the daytime.

By approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or by eating their food, or by accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them].
A husband shall confine a corrupt wife in a single room;
she must perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.
If, however, she should become defiled after being approached by one of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and reciting [sacred texts] constantly for three years.
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who associate with the outcastes.
By associating with an outcast for a year—through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance—one becomes an outcast; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
Whichever of these [sinners] a man associates with by falling into their company,
he must perform that very person's penance for the sake of purification from that association.
The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day,
in the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.
A female slave should overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a dead person;
the kinsmen, together with her, shall remain in a state of impurity for a day and a night.
But from that point on, they should desist from conversing with him, sitting together with him,
the giving of their inheritance, and even ordinary social intercourse.
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as shall the wealth obtainable by the eldest;
moreover, a younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the share of the eldest.
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe in a sacred body of water and together with him cast a new pitcher full of water into it.
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the duties of his kin as before.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they should live near the house.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins and have not been purified;
yet, once they have undergone purification, one should never despise them.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they have been purified according to the law.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and being abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform expiation.
When Brāhmaṇas acquire wealth through a censurable occupation,
they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by silent recitation and austerity.
Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
But when he has returned from the cow-pasture, emaciated by fasting and bowing before them, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (Manu 11.195)
But having spoken the truth before Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for cows;
once the sacred water-hole has been opened by the cows, they should perform his formal acceptance of it.
Having performed sacrifices for Vratyas, having performed funeral rites for others,
and having performed malevolent magic or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes that sin by three Kṛcchra penances.
Having abandoned one who has sought refuge or having caused the Veda to be lost,
a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
or by a human, a horse, a camel, or a pig, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month, or the recitation of the Saṃhitā,
as well as all the daily fire-oblations, are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals.
Having intentionally mounted a carriage drawn by camels or a carriage drawn by donkeys,
a Brahmin who has bathed while naked becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
If one is afflicted while away from water or even within water, or after having relieved the body's needs,
one becomes pure by bathing outside with one's clothes on and touching a cow.
If one neglects the obligatory rites prescribed in the Vedas,
or violates the vows of a *snātaka*, the expiation is fasting.
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" and an elder with "thou," one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and seek their favor by offering salutations.
Even after striking him with a blade of grass, or binding him by the neck with a cloth,
or defeating him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by prostrating before him.
But by merely threatening a Brahmin, or by striking him even once, or by intending to kill him, one falls into hell for a hundred or a thousand years.
As many particles of dust as the blood collects upon the surface of the earth,
for so many thousands of years shall the one who caused it remain in hell.
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.
But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
I shall describe to you those means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors, by which a human being removes his sins.

For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, for three days he should eat food obtained unasked, and for the next three days he should not eat at all; thus a twice-born man performs the Prājāpatya penance.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a fast for one night, is known as the *Sāṃtapanakṛcchra*.
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat only a single morsel for three periods of three days each as before, and should fast for the final three days. (Manu 11.213)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind.
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is the penance known as Parāka; it removes all sins.
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three periods of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, beginning with the bright fortnight and remaining self-restrained, should carry out this entire procedure in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama variety.
Restraining his self and subsisting on sacrificial food, one performing the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached midday. *Manu Smṛti* 11.218 [217M].
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating three hundred and sixty morsels of sacrificial food with a concentrated mind in this manner for one month, he attains the same world as the Moon.
The Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus,
and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
One should personally perform the fire-oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water while still wearing his clothes;
and he should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable to do so, he may lie on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of vows, honoring his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and other purificatory texts according to his ability;
for in all such vows, one who is intent on performing expiation should act in this manner.
The twice-born whose sins have been made public shall be purified by these vows;
however, those whose sins have not been made public, one should purify with sacred mantras and burnt offerings.
By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act, confesses it,
to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its slough.
To the extent that his mind reproaches the evil deed he has committed,
to that same extent his body is liberated from that unrighteousness.
For having committed a sin, one is indeed liberated from that sin by feeling remorse;
however, he is purified through the resolve of abstention, thinking, "I shall not do this again."
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform auspicious deeds through the activities of his mind, speech, and body.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable act, one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time. (Manu 11.232)
In whatever action he has committed that causes unease in his mind,
he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction.
All happiness, whether divine or human, has austerity as its root;
it is declared by the wise who perceive the Vedas that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.
For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge; for a Kṣatriya, austerity is protection;
for a Vaiśya, austerity is trade and agriculture; and for a Śūdra, austerity is service.
Sages who have restrained their selves and subsist on fruits, roots,
and air perceive the three worlds, with all that is mobile and immobile, through austerity alone.
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of divine power—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is indeed their means of attainment.
Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—
all this can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.
Even those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and others who have performed forbidden acts are liberated from that transgression through well-performed austerity alone.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even immobile beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.
Whatever sin people commit through their thoughts, words, or physical actions,
those whose wealth is austerity burn it all away instantly by means of austerity alone.
The gods accept the sacrifices of a Brahmin purified solely by austerity, and they fulfill his desires. (Manu 11.242)
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity.
Thus, the gods proclaim this to be the great power of austerity,
seeing the supreme merit of this entire austerity.
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices,
and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes.
Just as fire consumes whatever fuel it encounters in an instant by its heat,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge.
Thus has the expiation for these offenses been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret sins.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the syllable Om,
performed day after day, purify even the killer of an embryo within a month.
By muttering the *kautsa* hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the verse of Vasiṣṭha beginning with "prati," the *māhitra*,
and the *śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa hymns even once,
one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant.
Having repeated the Haviṣpāntīya hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and having recited the Puruṣa Sūkta, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from sin.
Desiring the removal of gross and subtle sins,
one should mutter for a year either the verse beginning with "Having known" (avet) or that beginning with "Whatever this" (yat kiṃ cedam).
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
But one who has committed many sins is purified by performing the Soma-Raudra rite for a month,
or by bathing in a flowing river while reciting the three verses beginning with "aryamṇām."

One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "Indra" for half a year; but having performed an act that is not praiseworthy, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.
Having offered clarified butter for a year with the Śākala-homa mantras, a twice-born man destroys even a very heavy sin; or he does so by reciting the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "namaḥ."
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year and subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.
Or, having purified himself with three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest; he is released from all sins. (Manu 11.258)
If one, being self-controlled, fasts for three days and approaches water three times a day,
he is released from all sins by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, removes all sins,
so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins.
Even if he has slain these three worlds and eats food from anywhere at all,
a Brahmin who retains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
Having recited the *Ṛgveda* collection three times, or the *Yajurveda*, or the *Sāmaveda* along with its secret portions, with a concentrated mind, one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does every evil deed sink away when one knows the threefold Veda.
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the various Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
The first is that Brahman consisting of three syllables, in which the triple Veda is established;
it is another secret threefold Veda—whosoever knows that is a knower of the Veda.
O sinless one, you have declared this entire dharma for the four castes;
now tell us truly the supreme outcome of the fruits of actions.
That righteous Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action."
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious;
the destinies of men, whether superior, inferior, or middling, are born of action.

One should know that for this embodied being—who possesses these three types [of action], who has three bases, and who is endowed with ten characteristics—it is the mind that is the instigator. (Mn 12.4)
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— this threefold action is mental.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and idle chatter—these constitute the fourfold nature of speech. (Mn 12.6)
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the rules, and adultery with another's wife—this is declared to be the threefold bodily [action]. (Manu 12.7)
This person experiences the auspicious and inauspicious results of mental action by means of the mind alone;
likewise, verbal action is experienced through speech, and bodily action through the body itself.
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or wild animals; and through those of the mind, to the status of a person of the lowest caste.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a "triple-staffed" ascetic (tridaṇḍin).
Having laid down this triple staff among all beings and having restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.
That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise.
The inner self, known as the *jīva*, is distinct and innate to all embodied beings;
it is by means of this that one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout births.
Both of these— the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)— being joined with the elements,
abide pervading that which exists within high and low beings.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from those very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment.
Having experienced those torments with this very body in the world of Yama,
they dissolve respectively back into those same elemental constituents.
Having experienced those defects born of attachment to sense objects, which result in unhappiness,
he approaches those same two of great splendor with his impurities removed.
Vigilantly observing both his merit and his sin together,
he perceives that which, when joined with them, brings him happiness or misery both in this world and after death.
If he practices dharma for the most part and adharma only to a small degree,
he enjoys happiness in heaven, enveloped by those very same elements.
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and righteousness only to a small degree,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from impurity,
returns again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.

Having observed these destinies of the living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self;
pervaded by these, the Great One (*mahat*) stands encompassing all these states without exception.
Whichever of these qualities predominates entirely within the body at any given time,
it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is said to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive form, which rests within all beings.
In that state, whatever one perceives within oneself as joined with joy,
tranquil and radiant with purity— that should be understood as *sattva*.
But that which is associated with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know that to be *rajas*, which is constantly carrying away embodied beings against their will.
But that which is conjoined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects,
inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
Furthermore, I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— whether they be superior, middling, or inferior.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses,
performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Delight in undertaking tasks, lack of fortitude, engagement in improper actions,
and constant indulgence in sensual objects are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
mendicancy, and negligence are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Moreover, for these three qualities abiding in the three [states],
this should be known as the summary definition of their characteristics in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when about to do it—
all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world and does not grieve when it is not attained should be known as rajasic.
That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel ashamed to practice,
and that by which one’s own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic of the qualities of a virtuous being.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Among these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.
I shall now briefly describe, in their proper order, all those qualities by which each of these transmigrates through the cycles of existence.
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is the threefold destiny.
This secondary course of existence should be understood as being threefold and of three kinds—
namely, inferior, middling, and superior— according to the specific nature of one's actions and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts— this is the lowest state of existence, characterized by darkness (tāmasī gati).
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati).
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, deceitful men,
Rākṣasas, and Piśācas constitute the highest state among those belonging to Tamas.
Jhallas, Mallas, actors, men who live by the sword,
and those addicted to gambling and drinking— this is the lowest state belonging to the quality of passion (rājasa).
Kings, Kṣatriyas, the domestic priests of kings,
and those who specialize in verbal warfare constitute the intermediate Rājasa path.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, find their highest state among those belonging to the Rajas quality.
Ascetics, self-restrained practitioners, Brahmins, the hosts of celestial beings in their aerial chariots,
the lunar mansions, and the Daityas— this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, sattvic goal.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—
these the wise declare to be the highest state characterized by sattva.
Thus has been fully described the entire cycle of worldly existence, consisting of all beings, which arises from the threefold action and is itself of three kinds and threefold.
Through attachment to the senses and by not practicing the Dharma,
the ignorant and lowest of men go to evil transmigrations.
Learn now all the various wombs into which this living soul enters in this world, one after another, according to its respective actions. Mn 12.53.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations upon the exhaustion of that [karmic residue].
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa. (Manu Smṛti 12.55)
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures. (Manu Smṛti 12.56)
A Brahmin who is a thief [becomes] thousands of times a spider, a snake, a lizard, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas. (Manu Smṛti 12.57)
The violator of the Guru’s bed becomes, by hundreds, [the body] of grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as of carnivorous animals, fanged beasts, and those who perform cruel deeds.

Those who eat the wives of others become carnivorous beasts of prey; those who steal become worms that feed on impure matter; and those who consort with women of the lowest castes become creatures that devour one another after death.
By entering into association with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by seizing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
A man who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, corals,
and various other jewels, is born among the workers in gold.

By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing meat, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [eats] meat, a cormorant fat, a *tailapaka* bird oil, a cricket salt, and a crane curd. (Mn 12.63)
Having stolen silk, a partridge [becomes so]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; for stealing a cow, an iguana; and for stealing molasses, a guḍa-bird.
The chuchundarī feeds on auspicious fragrances; the peacock, on leafy vegetables;
the porcupine, on various kinds of prepared food; and the śalyaka, on unprepared food.
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder wasp; and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [destroys] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruits and roots;
a bear, a woman; a cuckoo, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock.
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property,
or having consumed an offering that has not been consecrated by sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
Women also, by stealing in this same manner, incur guilt;
they become wives to these very same creatures.
For when the castes fall from their respective duties in times of no distress,
they undergo sinful transmigrations and fall into servitude under enemies.
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta with an emaciated face that eats vomit;
a Kṣatriya becomes a kaṭapūtana who eats impure matter and corpses.
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Maitrākṣajyotika who feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
To whatever extent those whose nature is directed toward sense objects indulge in them,
to that same extent skillfulness arises in them regarding those very objects.
Due to the repetition of those evil deeds, those of small intelligence encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world.
And there is the tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
as well as the forests of sword-leaves and the like, and the binding and cutting.
And various torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand mixed with grit, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he experiences births in various non-womb-born states that are mostly full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears.
Repeatedly dwelling in the womb, experiencing dreadful births,
various forms of bondage, and even the state of being a servant to others.
Separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people;
the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies.
And likewise, old age which is beyond remedy, the affliction by various diseases,
those manifold sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action,
with a body of that same nature one experiences its corresponding fruit.
Thus has been fully declared to you the arising of the fruits of all actions;
now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
And among all these auspicious actions here,
some particular action has been declared to be more conducive to the highest good for a person.
And among all these, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme;
for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained through it.
Of all these six types of actions, however, it should be known that the Vedic rite is always more conducive to welfare, both in this world and after death.
But in the Vedic path of action, all these [stages] without exception are included in their proper sequence within each respective ritual injunction.
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, being either active (pravṛtta) or withdrawn (nivṛtta).
Action performed with desire for results in this world or the next is called "pravṛtta" (active);
but action free from desire, preceded by knowledge, is taught as "nivṛtta" (withdrawn).
By practicing active karma, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renounced karma, one indeed transcends the five elements.
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self,
he who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty.
Even after abandoning the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
having attained this, a twice-born man has truly accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.
The Veda is the eternal eye of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all those are fruitless after death, for they are declared to have darkness as their ultimate goal.
Whatever other things besides these arise and pass away,
they are fruitless and false because they belong to the past.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately—
the past, the present, and the future— all are established from the Veda.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are produced from the Veda alone; their manifestation arises from the qualities and actions [of the elements].
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all living beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a person's purpose.
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a judge, and even lordship over all the world.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does one who knows the Veda burn away the defects of his own actions born of karma.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, residing in whichever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

Those who have studied the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely study them; those who possess true knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who act with resolve are superior to those who possess knowledge.
Austerity and sacred knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity he destroys evil, and through knowledge he partakes of immortality.
One who desires purity in dharma should thoroughly understand this triad: direct perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions. (Manu Smṛti 12.105)
He who examines the instruction on dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows dharma, and no other.
This action leading to supreme bliss has been declared in its entirety;
now the secret of this treatise of Manu is being taught.
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those duties not explicitly prescribed,
that which learned Brahmins declare shall be the law, free from doubt.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered in accordance with the Dharma,
are to be known as cultured Brahmins, who are the authorities for the Vedas and direct perception.
Whatever legal matter an assembly of at least ten members may determine,
or even one of at least three who are firm in their conduct, that law shall not be overturned.
One who is learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the three [other] members of the previous stages of life— this assembly shall consist of at least ten members.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this assembly of at least three is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding dharma.
Whatever Dharma even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Vedas may determine, that should be known as the supreme Dharma, not that which is proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.
Even if thousands of those who lack vows, lack sacred mantras, and subsist merely by their birth should assemble together, they do not constitute an assembly.
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, proclaim as such,
that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after those who spoke it.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of dharma.
Composed in meditation, one should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within oneself;
for by perceiving everything within oneself, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
One should place the ether within the cavities, the wind within the organs of movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, the waters within moisture, and the earth within the solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the steps,
Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call this Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self in all beings by means of his own self,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state.
A twice-born man who recites this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal.
